  • Task shape predicts the best architecture. Across 260 agent configurations, coordination helped decomposable tasks (up to +81%) and hurt strictly sequential ones (down to −70%). A model built on task features (sequential dependence, tool density) picked the best architecture for 87% of held-out cases. Centralized coordination contained error amplification far better than independent peers (Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems, 2025).
  • Adaptive collaboration beats a fixed team. MDAgents rates question complexity and routes to a solo agent or to progressively larger teams; it was best on 7 of 10 (medical) benchmarks (NeurIPS 2024). Tiered oversight escalates only on explicit triggers (TAO, 2025).
  • Debate is not a free upgrade. Multi-agent debate does not reliably beat a single agent with self-consistency (ICML 2024, 2025, NeurIPS 2025), and agent teams show authority bias and agents restating their opening positions (MedAgentAudit, 2025). Debate pays off for ranking hypotheses (AI co-scientist) and for specific contested claims.
  • Decide architecture first, then specialists, then depth (MasRouter, ACL 2025); bootstrap router labels from which route actually succeeded (Adaptive-RAG, NAACL 2024).

So Auto scores every architecture from the question's shape, explains the score, adjudicates only close calls, escalates on explicit triggers, and learns from how its answers held up.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
All five architectures run on one engine: the framework id only selects which agent phases run at each stage (tribos/agentic/runtime.py:get_phases). Auto therefore needs no new pipeline:

question ─► read_question (entities, intents, scope)
              │
              ├─ deterministic signals ─┐
              ├─ semantic features ─────┼─► blended features ─► scores (+ learned nudge) ─► softmax ─► guardrails
              │   (model, k samples)    │                                                              │
              └─ outcome history ───────┘                     close call? ─► model adjudication ◄──────┘
                                                                              │
                                   chosen framework's phases ─► first draft ─► ESCALATION (once) ─► critic debate
                                                                                                     │
                                   verification, claim confidence, task status ─► outcome store ◄────┘
  1. Features (tribos/agentic/router.py), each in [0, 1]: hypothesis generation, contested claim, safety-critical, asks for a recommendation, head-to-head comparison, target evaluation, exploratory, open-ended, computational, explicit parts, independent (decomposable) parts, sequential steps, several facets, several domains.
  2. Deterministic signals come from the planner's query context and keyword patterns.
  3. Semantic features come from one structured model call ([phase:router]) that reads the question's shape: question kind (proof, derivation, symbolic solve, numerical computation, simulation, parameter estimation, design and sizing, method comparison, safety and compliance, materials or reference lookup, hypothesis generation, conjecture, data analysis, literature review, exploration), number of parts, decomposable versus sequential, domains, and the flags above. TRIBOS_ROUTER_SAMPLES (1–5) averages several samples (self-consistency).
  4. The blend is 65% semantic, 35% deterministic. Safety flags (safety-critical, computational) are OR-ed: the model can raise them but never clear them. Without a model the deterministic signals are used alone.
  5. Scores. Each architecture's score is a weighted sum of the features (score_terms), grounded in the evidence above: plan & execute is the backbone and takes decomposable and computational work; debate takes hypotheses and contested conclusions, more strongly with stakes, a recommendation or a comparison; the supervisor takes open-ended, multi-facet questions without explicit parts; the swarm takes only low-stakes exploration. A softmax (temperature 0.4) gives a probability per architecture; the top probability is the router's confidence.
  6. Outcome learning (tribos/agentic/router_store.py). Every agentic research run, Auto-routed or chosen by the user, stores its features, a coarse question signature (kind plus strong flags), the architecture and an outcome quality: 35% grounding (verification score), 35% calibrated answer confidence, 15% task completion, 15% core phase health. Runs the user routed by hand observe architectures Auto did not pick. At routing time each architecture's mean quality on the same signature is shrunk toward its global mean (5 pseudo-runs), compared with the mean over all architectures, and added to its score (at least 3 runs, at most ±0.6). Only features are stored, never the question.
  7. Guardrails and adjudication. A safety-critical question is never routed to the swarm. When the top probability is under 50% and the runner-up is within 20 points, one model call ([phase:router_adjudicate]) picks between the two; any failure keeps the scored choice.
  8. Escalation (EscalationPhase, after the first draft, at most once, Auto only). The draft goes to a critic debate when model-judged counter-evidence contradicts it, the question is safety-critical, the route was uncertain (under 45%), the core phase fell back to a fixed plan, or at least two and more than half of the sub-questions still lack evidence, provided at least four agent model calls remain. The run keeps its architecture.
  9. Explanation. The router emits a "Choosing the approach" step and records execution_artifacts.framework_routing: chosen architecture, confidence, probabilities, the factors behind the score, the semantic reading, learned nudges, guardrail, adjudication and escalation. The Agent run card shows them under "Why this approach".

Settings: TRIBOS_ROUTER_LLM (off = deterministic only), TRIBOS_ROUTER_SAMPLES, TRIBOS_ROUTER_LEARNING (off | auto | on), TRIBOS_ROUTER_DIR.

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
scripts/eval_router.py routes the labelled question sets in tests/fixtures/routing/ and prints strict accuracy (the gold architecture), acceptable accuracy (gold or a listed alternative), accuracy per question kind and every miss:

  • benchmark.json: 60 engineering, physics and mathematics questions across 20 question kinds.
  • holdout.json: 24 questions written independently and never used for tuning, so its score is the honest one.

Both sets replaced the earlier clinical questions (2026-11-06) when Tribos became STEM-only; the router's weights were not re-tuned on them. Deterministic signals only, measured 2026-11-06:

Set Strict Acceptable Benchmark (60) 86.7% 98.3% Held-out (24) 87.5% 100%

The one wrong route: "Is it true that every bounded sequence of real numbers converges?" goes to debate (read as a contested claim) instead of plan & execute. The rest of the strict misses are acceptable alternatives: broad "overview / landscape / assess" questions go to plan & execute where the supervisor is preferred, because the keyword signals do not see their facets; the semantic features (below) are meant to supply that.

python scripts/eval_router.py                         # deterministic signals, benchmark
python scripts/eval_router.py --set holdout           # deterministic signals, held-out set
python scripts/eval_router.py --semantic --samples 3  # with the model's semantic features (needs a model key)

History: on the retired clinical sets, measured 2026-10-18 (semantic features from nvidia/nemotron-3-super-120b-a12b, one sample):

Router Benchmark strict / acceptable Held-out strict / acceptable Deterministic signals only 95.0% / 100% 83.3% / 95.8% Flat 65/35 blend of semantic and deterministic features 83.3% / 86.7% 87.5% / 91.7% Per-feature trust (current) 96.7% / 98.3% 87.5% / 95.8%

The flat blend was worse: the model over-called "exploratory", "open-ended" and "needs computation" on plain lookups and diluted precise keyword hits. Per-feature trust (keyword hits stand, model-only specialist flags are discounted, structural features lean on the model) fixed that. The held-out set was inspected after the flat-blend run, so its current score is slightly optimistic. Remaining misses are "explore the links between X, Y and Z" questions, which the model reads as multi-part and routes to plan & execute rather than the swarm.

tests/test_auto_router.py guards the deterministic accuracy on both sets, and covers semantic features, self-consistency, guardrails, adjudication, outcome learning, escalation and Auto end to end. The labels encode the routing policy, not measured answer quality; the outcome store is what ties routing to how answers actually held up.

docs.title: Context gate, the Lumo Admission Gate and concise answers
docs.text: What reaches the answer model, how long the answer is, and what is never sent at all. Code: context_gate.py, wired in prompts.py (build_evidence_block, CONCISE_ANSWER_RULE) and plan.py (stage 0.12).

docs.title: 1. Query-focused extractive compression
docs.text:
Retrieved literature passages are split into sentences, ranked by BM25 against the question across all retrieved sentences, and only the most relevant ones are kept (at most 6 per passage, TRIBOS_CONTEXT_GATE_CHARS in total, default 6000), in their original order. Nothing is paraphrased, so citations stay exact.

Why: extractive compression of retrieved documents keeps question-answering accuracy at a fraction of the tokens (RECOMP, Xu, Shi & Choi, ICLR 2024; here the scorer is lexical BM25, Robertson & Zaragoza 2009, so it needs no model); long contexts also degrade use of what is in them ("Lost in the Middle", Liu et al., TACL 2024).

When no sentence matches the question, the passages are excerpted as before, so an answer never loses its evidence.

docs.title: 2. The Lumo Admission Gate
docs.text:
Standalone package: Lumo-GATE. Every kept sentence gets an integer admission score K:

Source class Weight Tribos sources official +3 technical reports and standards; standards and regulatory hosts internal +2 peer-reviewed journals and conferences, textbooks and reference works; repository, publisher and university hosts external +1 preprints; other web pages unverified 0 forums and social media false −3 retracted papers

K = the sentence's own weight + the weight of every other independent source stating the same fact − the weight of every reliable source stating a conflicting value. Only K ≥ 1 is admitted; K = 0 is quarantined and K ≤ −1 blocked (counted in the run trace, never shown to the model). Two pages of one source count once.

For scientific text, the word-overlap relation needs 80% shared words for a conflict, and when sentences carry several numbers, some must be shared (the conditions) while others differ. "100 °C at 1 atm" and "120 °C at 2 atm" are different conditions, not a conflict; "100 °C at 1 atm" and "105 °C at 1 atm" are.

Honest limits: K is only as good as the source classes behind it, and the word-overlap relation is crude. What the gate implements is source-weighted corroboration with abstention, in line with grounding research (attributable answers, ALCE, Gao et al., EMNLP 2023). Claim-level checking of the written answer stays with the existing verifier.

docs.title: 3. The paradox guard
docs.text: A self-referential statement ("this statement is false") has no grounding context (K = 0) and is answered at once with a fixed explanation, before the planner, any source, tool or model call: 0 model requests, about 1 s.

docs.title: 4. Concise answers
docs.text: TRIBOS_ANSWER_STYLE=concise (the default) asks the writer for the direct answer first and only the steps, values and evidence that support it; a requested proof or derivation is still given in full. full restores the longer report format. Asking for brevity cuts output without losing accuracy on reasoning tasks (Nayab et al., "Concise Thoughts", arXiv:2407.19825, 2024).

docs.title: 5. Do what was asked, no more
docs.text:
• Lean only on request. TRIBOS_FORMAL_MODE=explicit (default): a machine-checked Lean proof is attempted when the question asks for one ("formal proof", "in Lean", "machine-checked", "formally verify"); "prove that ..." gets a written proof. auto restores Lean for every proof question.
  • Rewrite rounds stop when the answer has converged: a round that changed less than 5% of the text ends the loop (measured on a comparison question: rounds changed 14%, then 3%, each resending ~30k characters). In concise mode, medium effort allows at most 1 rewrite round and high 2.
  • Generative UI. The writer picks the form that shows the answer best: prose for a one-line answer; otherwise up to three blocks: stats (headline numbers), steps (a procedure or short derivation), table (a comparison), chart (a trend whose points are in the computed results or evidence), equation (the key formula) and callout (one caveat). Every number in a block must appear in the answer or the evidence, or the block is removed; a writer's equation never carries "passed" checks (only computed results do).

Measured on "Compare the density, Young's modulus and yield strength of aluminium 6061, steel S355 and titanium Ti-6Al-4V" (medium): 196 s → 104 s, 394 → 267 words, no rewrite round needed, 2 of 2 checked claims supported.

docs.title: 6. Prompt caching
docs.text: The answer instructions (about 2,270 tokens) are a fixed prefix of every answer call, so Meta's API caches them (measured: 2,161 of 2,271 prompt tokens cached on a repeat). Keep anything that varies per question after the fixed instructions, never before them.

docs.title: Measured (medium effort, muse-spark-1.3, scripts/measure_tokens.py)
docs.text:
Question Answer words Time Characters sent Boiling point of water at 2 atm 137 → 15 13.5 → 9.6 s 13,000 → 13,700 How CRISPR-Cas9 causes off-target edits and how they are reduced 1,001 → 442 50.7 → 31.8 s 37,600 → 27,000 Solve x² − 5x + 6 = 0 78 → 66 11.2 → 10.9 s 14,000 → 14,600

On the literature question the gate kept 35 of 105 sentences (66% less evidence text) and all 6 checked claims were supported. Run python scripts/measure_tokens.py --out after.json --compare before.json to repeat the comparison.

docs.title: Reading question images
docs.text: A question sent as a photo, scan, screenshot or PDF is turned into Markdown with LaTeX before it is solved (POST /api/vision/read, tribos/vision/). Mathematics is where single engines fail. OCR reads (∀)i∈ℕ* as (V)ieN* and a_i ≡ a_j (mod a_k) as a1 = a3 (mod ax), and a vision model on its own sometimes drops a line or misreads an index. So images are read by an ensemble, and every engine's output is checked against the others.

docs.title: The pipeline
docs.text:
Step Engine What it contributes 1a Indra OCR (ocr.py; local CPU, ONNX) Layout and lines, with formulas as LaTeX drafts 1b Tesseract (tesseract.py; local) Plain words, each with a confidence (printed words 90+, garbled math near 0) 2a Vision reading, image only (vlm.transcribe_remote) Started at once, alongside OCR 2b Vision reading, with both OCR drafts A second reading by the same model with different input: it catches many of 2a's slips, but the two are not independent 3 Agreement (consensus.compare) The two readings are compared in canonical form 4 Review (vlm.review_remote) Only when the readings differ: the model looks at the image again at each listed difference 5 Coverage gate and repair (consensus.coverage, vlm.repair_remote) The result must keep the words that are surely in the image

Canonical form. Unicode math becomes LaTeX commands (∀ → \forall), aliases get one spelling (\ne → \neq, \le → \leq, \bmod/\pmod{m} → (mod m)), and grouping braces, spacing, \left/\right, \text{} wrappers and Markdown emphasis are dropped. Set braces count only where they are printed: {a_n} in text equals \{a_n\} in math. What still differs after this is a real difference in what was read (a_i against a_1, \equiv against =).

Words surely in the image. These are the words Tesseract read with confidence ≥ 80 that Indra also read; when there are too few of them, Tesseract's confident words alone, then Indra's words of four letters or more. Digits glued to letters (a1, a misread subscript) and garbled tokens never count. A transcription has to keep at least 75% of these words. One that keeps fewer is read again once, and the model is told which words are missing. If the second reading still misses them, the OCR text is shown with a warning, so no line is lost silently. Before this gate existed, garbled OCR tokens counted as required words, and an exact transcription was rejected because it "kept 40%".

Independence. Both vision readings and the review come from one model, so their agreement is self-consistency, not independent confirmation. The independent evidence is the two OCR engines, which the coverage gate uses.

Outcome. Each reading reports consensus: - agreed: the two readings (same model, different inputs) matched; - settled: they differed, and a look at the image decided each place; - unsettled: the review was unusable, so the reader is warned; - single: there was only one usable reading.

The reading also lists the differences that were found, and the unconfirmed_numbers that no OCR engine read. The image viewer in the composer shows these.

Small images. An image whose long side is under 1000 px is enlarged for the vision model, by up to 3x to at most 1280 px. A vision encoder samples its input at a fixed resolution. Before this change, a 464×50 screenshot gave each glyph a few pixels, and the two readings misread different symbols (x_i^n for x_i, +\infty for \infty). With the enlargement, the same images read exactly. The OCR engines upscale small images for the same reason.

Latency (measured on this machine against the cloud model): - Indra takes about 0.3 s and Tesseract about 0.5 s, in parallel threads. - A reading takes 3.5 to 7 s when the two readings agree. - Settling a difference adds 3 to 8 s. - The first image after a restart also loads Indra's models, which takes about 2 s.

TRIBOS_VISION_CROSSCHECK=0 turns off the second reading and the review.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: Variable Default Purpose TRIBOS_VISION_PROVIDER remote remote (the full ensemble), ollama (one local model reading), ocr (OCR only; the image stays on the machine) TRIBOS_VISION_MODEL muse-spark-1.3 The cloud vision model TRIBOS_VISION_CROSSCHECK true The second reading and the review TRIBOS_VISION_TESSERACT unset The Tesseract executable. It is found on PATH, in Scoop or in Program Files when unset; off disables it TRIBOS_VISION_TESSERACT_LANG eng Tesseract language models, for example eng+deu TRIBOS_VISION_OCR_MATH true Indra's math models

docs.title: Installing Tesseract
docs.text:
Tesseract is optional: without it, the gate falls back to Indra's longer words. With it, the gate is far more reliable.

  • Windows: run scoop install tesseract. Then put eng.traineddata from tessdata_best in ~/scoop/persist/tesseract/tessdata/. Alternatively, winget install UB-Mannheim.TesseractOCR installs it to C:\Program Files\Tesseract-OCR.
  • Debian/Ubuntu: run apt-get install tesseract-ocr tesseract-ocr-eng. The backend Docker image already includes these.
  • macOS: run brew install tesseract.

GET /api/vision/status reports word_recognition: true once Tesseract and its language model are found.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
• tests/test_feat_vision_ensemble.py covers the reported failure, using the real OCR output. It also covers canonical agreement and real differences, the review and its guard, the repair, and partial failures.
  • tests/test_vision.py covers the endpoint, the PDFs, the cache and the fallbacks.

docs.title: Agent platform API
docs.text:
Run control, background jobs, research projects, the MCP server and the A2A endpoint (features 13, 15, 16, 17 of docs/plans/agentic-system.md). All routes use the same bearer authentication as /api/chat (TRIBOS_API_TOKENS, TRIBOS_JWT_SECRET, or TRIBOS_AUTH_MODE=disabled for local development) and are scoped to the authenticated user: another user's run, job, project or task id answers exactly like an unknown one (404, or JSON-RPC -32001 for A2A).

The examples use TOKEN for a bearer token and http://localhost:8000 for the backend.

docs.title: SSE events added by agentic runs
docs.text:
Agentic frameworks (agentic-plan-execute, multi-agent-supervisor, multi-agent-swarm, multi-agent-debate) add two event types to the chat stream (POST /api/chat/stream) and to job event logs. All other event types (init, thought, reasoning_delta, content_delta, content_reset, done, error) are unchanged.

Event When Shape run_control first event of an agentic run {"type":"run_control","run_id":"run_…","framework":"agentic-plan-execute","interactive":true} approval_request a phase waits for the researcher {"type":"approval_request","run_id","approval_id":"apr_…","kind":"plan"\|"dag","payload":{…}} job job status change (job logs only) {"type":"job","job_id","status","run_id"?,"resumed"?}

A plan approval payload:

{
  "sources": [
    {"key": "archivon", "label": "Scholarly literature search (Archivon, arXiv, Europe PMC)", "run": true, "reason": ""},
    {"key": "websurfer", "label": "Web search", "run": true, "reason": ""},
    {"key": "dynamis", "label": "Dynamical simulation (Dynamis, SciPy)", "run": false, "reason": "no simulation requested"}
  ],
  "expensive": ["parameter scan"],
  "question": "..."
}

Legacy alias keys (lithoscribe, vivarix) and tools this installation does not have are never listed; switching a source off also switches off its alias. A source the plan skipped (run: false) cannot be switched on from the card.

Plan approval runs on interactive runs when agent_options.require_plan_approval is set or expensive work is routed (simulation, parameter scan, single-cell analysis, calibration, docking, sandboxed analysis). A non-interactive run with require_plan_approval is approved automatically and recorded as auto. With no answer within TRIBOS_APPROVAL_TIMEOUT_S (default 300 s) the plan runs as proposed (timeout).

A clarifying question ends the turn instead: the response is the question with numbered options, task_status.task_status is needs_input, and the artifact clarification is {"question","options","reason","signals"}. The next message in the thread is treated as the answer ("2" or the option text): it is merged with the original question, and the agent never asks twice in a row.

docs.title: Run control: /api/agent/runs/{run_id}
docs.text:
Method Path Body Result GET /api/agent/runs/{run_id} {"run_id","interactive","cancelled","pending":[{approval_id,kind,payload,created}],"decisions":[…],"queued_steering"} POST /api/agent/runs/{run_id}/approve {"approval_id","approved",payload?,message?} {"success":true,…}; 409 if the approval is no longer pending POST /api/agent/runs/{run_id}/steer {"message"} (at most 2000 characters) {"success":true,"queued_steering":n} POST /api/agent/runs/{run_id}/cancel {"reason"?} {"success":true,"cancelled":true} GET /api/agent/reliability tool reliability snapshot (circuit breakers, retries, cache) when available

Editing the plan can only switch sources off. Send the payload back with "run": false on the rows to drop (or {"sources": {"websurfer": false}}). Rejecting the plan ("approved": false) keeps only the literature search. The artifact plan_approval records {"approval_id","status":"approved|edited|rejected|auto|timeout", "sources","switched_off"}.

# approve the plan but switch the web search off
curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/agent/runs/run_0123456789abcdef/approve \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"approval_id":"apr_0123456789","approved":true,"payload":{"sources":{"websurfer":false}}}'

# add an instruction while the run is in progress (read before synthesis and after each draft)
curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/agent/runs/run_0123456789abcdef/steer \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"message":"Focus on pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma"}'

Run controls live in the server process; they disappear when the run ends.

docs.title: Background jobs: /api/jobs
docs.text:
A job runs one question without a client attached. The event log is durable (SQLite), ordered by seq, and can be replayed and followed.

Method Path Notes POST /api/jobs body = the /api/chat request fields → 201 {"job_id","run_id","status":"queued","thread_id"}; 429 over the per-user limit; a repeated client_request_id returns the same job (see below) GET /api/jobs ?status=&thread_id=&limit= → {"jobs":[…]} (no results in the list) GET /api/jobs/{id} the job with result (the chat response object), pending_approvals, watchers, last_seq GET /api/jobs/{id}/events SSE: replay ?after=N then follow; Last-Event-ID works; ?stream=false returns JSON POST /api/jobs/{id}/cancel queued: cancelled at once; running: cancelled at the next checkpoint POST /api/jobs/{id}/resume interrupted, failed or cancelled jobs run again (new run_id; tool calls hit the result cache) DELETE /api/jobs/{id} cancels if needed, then deletes the job and its log

Statuses: queued, running, waiting_approval, succeeded, failed, cancelled, interrupted. Jobs left running when the server stops are marked interrupted at the next start. Each SSE frame is id: <seq> plus data: <event JSON with "seq">. A : ping comment is sent while idle. The stream ends after the current attempt's done or error event. While a client is attached the run is interactive, so plan approvals wait for an answer through /api/agent/runs/{run_id}/approve. When the last watcher leaves, a pending approval is approved automatically.

curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/jobs -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"message":"Simulate a damped oscillator with m=1, c=0.4, k=4 and find its decay time.","framework":"agentic-plan-execute","agent_options":{"require_plan_approval":true}}'

# reattach after event 42
curl -N "http://localhost:8000/api/jobs/job_0123456789abcdef/events?after=42" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

A runtime api_key sent with a job is kept in memory only, never written to the job store. After a restart, a resumed job runs with the server's keys.

The stored request keeps message (the question as solved, with the transcriptions of attached images) and display_message (what the user typed): clients compare the thread's last user message with request.display_message ?? request.message when they reopen a job, so the question is not shown twice.

docs.title: Retries: client_request_id
docs.text:
POST /api/chat, POST /api/chat/stream and POST /api/jobs accept an optional client_request_id (1-100 characters of A-Z a-z 0-9 _ . : -, e.g. a UUID). A client generates one per question and sends the same id when it retries that question (for example the web app's JSON fallback after a dropped stream):

  • Chat: while a request with the same id is still running for the same user, the duplicate is refused with 409 ("This question is already running …") and takes no chat slot. The id is released when the run ends, so a retry after the first run finished or failed runs normally.
  • Jobs: a duplicate within 10 minutes returns the job the first request created (200, same job_id, plus "duplicate": true) instead of queueing the question twice; 409 while the first submission is still being stored.

Ids are kept per user in a bounded in-memory table (at most 32 ids per user, entries expire), so they are not shared between server processes and are forgotten on restart.

docs.title: Research projects: /api/projects
docs.text:
Method Path Body / query POST /api/projects {"name","description"} → 201 project (id = prj_…) GET /api/projects list with fact counts GET / PATCH / DELETE /api/projects/{id} PATCH {"name"?,"description"?}; DELETE removes the project and its facts GET /api/projects/{id}/memory ?query= ranked recall (what the agent would get), else newest first; include_invalid=true shows history PATCH /api/projects/{id}/memory/{fact_id} {"invalidate":true,"reason"} or an edit {"object"?,"value"?,"confidence"?,"verified"?,"tags"?}; unknown fields are refused with 422 DELETE /api/projects/{id}/memory/{fact_id} hard delete

Send project_id with a chat or job request to use the project's memory. A fact is {"id":"fct_…","subject","relation","object","value","valid_from","invalid_at","recorded_at","source":{"thread_id","run_id","tool"},"confidence","verified","tags"}. A contradiction (a new classification, mechanism or association score) invalidates the old fact and does not delete it. Editing an object or value creates a new version of the fact. Facts from turns that failed verification are tagged unverified. The artifact project_memory is {"project_id","recalled":[…],"written","invalidated"}.

docs.title: MCP server: POST /mcp
docs.text:
JSON-RPC 2.0 over Streamable HTTP. Responses are always JSON; GET /mcp returns 405. Supported protocol versions are 2026-07-28, 2025-11-25, 2025-06-18 and 2025-03-26. initialize echoes a supported client version and otherwise answers 2025-11-25. An unsupported MCP-Protocol-Version header (or _meta["io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion"]) is rejected with -32600.

Methods: initialize, notifications/initialized (202, no body), ping, server/discover, tools/list, tools/call. Error codes: -32700 parse error, -32600 invalid request, -32601 method not found, -32602 invalid params or unknown tool, -32603 internal error. A tool that runs and fails returns isError: true.

Tools: - tribos_research {question, framework?, enable_web_search?, thread_id?} runs the full orchestrator non-interactively. It returns the answer as text plus structuredContent {answer, citations, verification, task_status, framework, thread_id}. - Read-only registry tools from TRIBOS_MCP_TOOLS (comma-separated). The default list (DEFAULT_TOOLS in app/backend/routers/mcp.py) is the Archivon literature tools, the Axiom computer-algebra tools, the Dynamis simulation tools and the Physis reference-data tools, each when it is registered. Each inputSchema is the tool's pydantic schema. Tools whose names suggest writes, uploads, code execution, docking or generation are never exposed.

curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/mcp -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "MCP-Protocol-Version: 2025-11-25" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"axiom_solve","arguments":{"equations":"x^2 - 2 = 0","variables":"x","domain":"real"}}}'

Client configuration (Claude Desktop, Claude Code or any client that supports remote Streamable HTTP servers):

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "tribos": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "http://localhost:8000/mcp",
      "headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer YOUR_TRIBOS_TOKEN"}
    }
  }
}

Security, following Hou et al. 2025 (arXiv:2503.23278): - The tool allowlist is fixed. - No write tools are exposed. - Tool descriptions are static. - Bearer authentication is required. - Origin is checked against TRIBOS_CORS_ORIGINS plus TRIBOS_MCP_ALLOWED_ORIGINS (DNS-rebinding protection). - Each user can run at most TRIBOS_MCP_MAX_CONCURRENT (default 2) tools/call requests at once. - The server is stateless: no sessions and no sampling.

docs.title: A2A: /.well-known/agent-card.json and POST /a2a
docs.text:
The A2A v1.0.0 JSON-RPC binding (https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/specification/). The Agent Card is public. It lists the skills stem-research and symbolic-numerical-simulation, a bearer security scheme, and capabilities.streaming = false. Its URLs use TRIBOS_PUBLIC_URL when it is set (an http(s):// base URL, e.g. behind a reverse proxy), else the base URL of the request.

Methods: SendMessage, GetTask, ListTasks and CancelTask. The pre-1.0 aliases message/send, tasks/get, tasks/list and tasks/cancel are also accepted. Every message becomes a background job: - The task id is the job id and contextId is the thread. - status.state is one of submitted, working, input-required, completed, failed or canceled. - A completed task carries the answer as a text artifact. - configuration.blocking: true waits for the answer, up to TRIBOS_A2A_BLOCKING_TIMEOUT_S (default 300 s).

Errors: -32001 task not found, -32002 task not cancelable.

curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/a2a -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{
  "jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"SendMessage",
  "params":{"message":{"role":"user","messageId":"m1","parts":[{"kind":"text","text":"What is the period of a 2 kg mass on a 50 N/m spring?"}]},
            "configuration":{"blocking":true}}}'

docs.title: Environment
docs.text:
Variable Default Purpose TRIBOS_APPROVAL_TIMEOUT_S 300 how long a plan approval waits TRIBOS_JOBS_DIR $TRIBOS_RUNS_DIR/jobs, else data/jobs job store TRIBOS_JOB_WORKERS 2 asyncio job workers TRIBOS_MAX_JOBS_PER_USER 3 queued + running jobs per user TRIBOS_JOB_MAX_EVENTS 20000 log cap (token deltas are dropped past it) TRIBOS_JOB_CANCEL_GRACE_S 20 after this long a cancelled agentic job's task is cancelled outright TRIBOS_PROJECTS_DIR next to the research memory store project store TRIBOS_MCP_TOOLS built-in read-only list MCP registry-tool allowlist TRIBOS_MCP_MAX_CONCURRENT 2 concurrent MCP tools/call per user TRIBOS_MCP_ALLOWED_ORIGINS (none) extra allowed Origin values for /mcp TRIBOS_MCP_RESEARCH_TIMEOUT_S 900 tribos_research timeout TRIBOS_A2A_BLOCKING_TIMEOUT_S 300 blocking SendMessage wait TRIBOS_PUBLIC_URL (request base URL) base URL in the A2A Agent Card

Jobs and run controls assume one server process per jobs directory. Startup recovery marks every running job interrupted.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• CLAM (arXiv:2212.07769), Clarify When Necessary (arXiv:2311.09469), Aliannejadi et al. (arXiv:1907.06554): clarification.
  • Magentic-UI (arXiv:2507.22358): co-planning and action guards.
  • LangGraph persistence (https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/persistence): durable jobs. Living systematic reviews (Elliott et al. 2014, doi:10.1371/journal.pmed.1001603) motivate long-running research.
  • Zep (arXiv:2501.13956), Mem0 (arXiv:2504.19413), HippoRAG (arXiv:2405.14831), Generative Agents (arXiv:2304.03442), MemGPT (arXiv:2310.08560), A-MEM (arXiv:2502.12110): project memory.
  • MCP specification (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/, https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/), A2A specification (https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/specification/), Hou et al. 2025 (arXiv:2503.23278): interoperability and security.

docs.title: Tribos agentic features: verified literature (agent loop and reasoning)
docs.text: Every paper below was checked against its arXiv abstract or HTML page, an official proceedings page (PMLR, ICLR, ACL Anthology), or the bioRxiv PDF. Specific numbers (thresholds, prompts, counts) were read from the paper's full text, not just the abstract. Details marked "(confirm in PDF)" come from the paper body and were not re-read in this session. Check those before hard-coding them.

docs.title: 1. Dynamic plan-and-execute (DAG of tool calls, parallel execution, replanning)
docs.text:
• An LLM Compiler for Parallel Function Calling: Sehoon Kim et al., 2023 (v1 Dec 2023), ICML 2024. arXiv:2312.04511. https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.04511
  • Technique to borrow: this is the core design. A Planner LLM outputs numbered tasks forming a DAG. A dependent task refers to an earlier result with a placeholder ($1, $2). A Task Fetching Unit, which needs no LLM, sends out each task as soon as its dependencies resolve (greedy) and fills in the placeholders. An Executor runs ready tasks concurrently. For dynamic replanning, the Executor's results go back to the Planner, which emits a new task set, and this repeats until the final answer. Reported speedups over ReAct are 1.8x on HotpotQA, 3.74x on Movie Recommendation and 2.15x on ParallelQA (GPT). This maps directly onto parallel calls to EuropePMC, OpenTargets, ChEMBL and ClinicalTrials.gov.

  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.04511 and https://arxiv.org/html/2312.04511

  • ReWOO: Decoupling Reasoning from Observations for Efficient Augmented Language Models: Binfeng Xu et al., 2023, arXiv preprint (no venue listed). arXiv:2305.18323. https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18323

  • Technique to borrow: plan the whole tool chain up front, without waiting for observations. Planner, Worker and Solver are separate modules, with evidence variables #E1, #E2 (confirm in PDF). Reported results are about 5x token efficiency and +4% accuracy on HotpotQA. It also holds up when tools fail, and planning can be offloaded to a smaller model. Use it as the low-cost path when the query is predictable.

  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18323

  • Plan-and-Solve Prompting: Improving Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought Reasoning by Large Language Models: Lei Wang et al., 2023, ACL 2023. arXiv:2305.04091. https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.04091

  • Technique to borrow: the zero-shot planning trigger for the planner system prompt. PS: "Let's first understand the problem and devise a plan to solve the problem. Then, let's carry out the plan and solve the problem step by step." PS+ adds "extract relevant variables and their corresponding numerals" and "calculate intermediate variables (pay attention to correct numerical calculation and commonsense)".

  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/html/2305.04091

  • ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models: Shunyu Yao et al., 2022, ICLR 2023. arXiv:2210.03629. https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629

  • Technique to borrow: an interleaved Thought, Action, Observation loop. Use it as the fallback executor for steps whose next action depends on the last observation, and as the baseline that LLMCompiler and ReWOO are measured against. It cuts hallucination and error propagation compared with chain-of-thought (CoT) on HotpotQA and FEVER.
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629

docs.title: 2. Gap-driven iterative re-retrieval (find unanswered sub-questions after a draft, retrieve again within a budget)
docs.text:
• Active Retrieval Augmented Generation (FLARE): Zhengbao Jiang et al., 2023, EMNLP 2023. arXiv:2305.06983. https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.06983
  • Technique to borrow: forward-looking active retrieval. The model generates a tentative next sentence. If that sentence contains any low-confidence tokens (token probability below a threshold theta), the sentence is used as the query, or the low-confidence spans are masked or turned into questions (confirm in PDF). The system then retrieves and regenerates the sentence. Apply this per draft sentence to spot "gaps".

  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.06983

  • Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection: Akari Asai et al., 2023, ICLR 2024 (oral). arXiv:2310.11511. https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.11511

  • Technique to borrow: the reflection-token rubric, used as an LLM-judge schema without fine-tuning.
    • Retrieve = {yes, no, continue}
    • IsRel = {relevant, irrelevant}
    • IsSup = {fully, partially, no support}
    • IsUse = {1..5}
    • Segment score = p(segment) + sum of w_G * s_G over the critique tokens. Default weights are IsRel 1.0, IsSup 1.0 and IsUse 0.5.
    • A hard filter drops segments rated "no support".
    • A "partially/no support" verdict on a claim means a gap, which triggers another retrieval.

  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/html/2310.11511 and https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/hash/25f7be9694d7b32d5cc670927b8091e1-Abstract-Conference.html

  • Corrective Retrieval Augmented Generation (CRAG): Shi-Qi Yan et al., 2024, arXiv preprint (no venue listed). arXiv:2401.15884. https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.15884

  • Technique to borrow: a three-way action rule driven by a retrieval evaluator. The evaluator is a fine-tuned T5-large that scores each document from -1 to 1, compared against an upper and a lower threshold.
    • Correct: any document scores above the upper threshold. Refine the retrieved documents.
    • Incorrect: every document scores below the lower threshold. Discard them and fall back to web search.
    • Ambiguous: otherwise. Combine both sources.
    • Example thresholds: PopQA (0.59, -0.99); PubHealth (0.5, -0.91).
    • Decompose-then-recompose: split documents into strips, filter strips scoring below -0.5, keep the top 5, and concatenate them in order.
  • In Tribos, swap web search for a reformulated EuropePMC query.

  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/html/2401.15884

  • Language agents achieve superhuman synthesis of scientific knowledge (PaperQA2): Michael D. Skarlinski et al., 2024, arXiv preprint. arXiv:2409.13740. https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.13740

  • Technique to borrow: an agentic literature loop with four tools.
    • Paper Search: a keyword query returning 12 papers by default, then chunked and embedded.
    • Gather Evidence: dense top-k of 30 chunks, followed by RCS (reranking and contextual summarization). An LLM writes a short query-specific summary of each chunk and scores its relevance, and chunks are reranked by that score.
    • Citation Traversal: one hop to citing and cited papers, starting from papers whose summary scored 8 or higher, capped at 12 papers.
    • Generate Answer: uses the top 15 summaries by default. The authors found 5 gave the best accuracy.
  • The agent keeps calling Search, Gather and Traverse until it judges the evidence sufficient. This is the template for a budgeted re-retrieval loop over EuropePMC.

  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/html/2409.13740

  • Also verified, as a supporting reference: Interleaving Retrieval with Chain-of-Thought Reasoning for Knowledge-Intensive Multi-Step Questions (IRCoT): Harsh Trivedi et al., 2022, ACL 2023. arXiv:2212.10509. https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.10509

  • Technique to borrow: each new CoT sentence becomes the next retrieval query, and the retrieved passages feed the next reasoning step. This gives a simple per-step re-retrieval baseline.
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.10509

docs.title: 3. Question decomposition
docs.text:
• Least-to-Most Prompting Enables Complex Reasoning in Large Language Models: Denny Zhou et al., 2022, ICLR 2023. arXiv:2205.10625. https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.10625
  • Technique to borrow: two stages. First decompose the problem into an ordered list of simpler subproblems. Then solve them in order, adding each answer to the context for the next one. Use this for sequential biomedical chains, for example target, then pathway, then compound, then trial.

  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.10625

  • Measuring and Narrowing the Compositionality Gap in Language Models (Self-Ask): Ofir Press et al., 2022, Findings of EMNLP 2023. arXiv:2210.03350. https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03350

  • Technique to borrow: the model explicitly asks and answers follow-up questions before giving the final answer. The scaffold is "Are follow up questions needed here: / Follow up: / Intermediate answer: / So the final answer is:" (confirm in PDF). Because the follow-ups are explicit, each "Follow up:" can go to a search tool, here EuropePMC or OpenTargets.

  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03350

  • Decomposed Prompting: A Modular Approach for Solving Complex Tasks: Tushar Khot et al., 2022, ICLR 2023. arXiv:2210.02406. https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.02406

  • Technique to borrow: a decomposer prompt sends sub-tasks to a library of sub-task handlers. Each handler can be another prompt, a further decomposition, a trained model or a symbolic function. Long inputs can be reduced recursively. This matches routing sub-questions to typed Tribos tools (ChEMBL lookup, COPASI simulation, Scanpy analysis).
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.02406

docs.title: 4. Multi-agent topologies (supervisor, swarm/handoffs, debate)
docs.text:
• Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate: Yilun Du et al., 2023, ICML 2024 (PMLR 235:11733-11763). arXiv:2305.14325. https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14325
  • Technique to borrow: the debate topology. By default, 3 agents debate for 2 rounds. In round 2 and later each agent sees: "These are the solutions to the problem from other agents: ... Using the opinion of other agents as additional advice, can you give an updated response ...". Rounds continue until the agents converge on a common answer. The method works with black-box models and uses the same prompts across tasks.

  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/html/2305.14325 and https://proceedings.mlr.press/v235/du24e.html

  • Magentic-One: A Generalist Multi-Agent System for Solving Complex Tasks: Adam Fourney et al., 2024, arXiv preprint. arXiv:2411.04468. https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.04468

  • Technique to borrow: the supervisor pattern with two ledgers.
    • Outer loop, Task Ledger: given or verified facts, facts to look up, facts to derive, educated guesses, and a plan.
    • Inner loop, Progress Ledger: answers five questions each step: (1) is the request satisfied, (2) are we looping, (3) are we making progress, (4) which agent speaks next, (5) what instruction to give it.
    • Stall counter: goes up on a loop or no progress. Above a threshold of 2, the orchestrator reflects, updates the Task Ledger and replans, and all agents reset their context.

  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/html/2411.04468

  • AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversation: Qingyun Wu et al., 2023, COLM 2024 (per Microsoft Research and AG2 listings; arXiv shows no journal-ref). arXiv:2308.08155. https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.08155

  • Technique to borrow: "conversable" agents that combine an LLM, tools and human input, with interaction patterns defined in code and natural language (group chat with a speaker selector, two-agent chats). This is the reference design for swarm and handoff-style topologies and human-proxy agents.

  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.08155 and https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/autogen-enabling-next-gen-llm-applications-via-multi-agent-conversation-framework/

  • MetaGPT: Meta Programming for A Multi-Agent Collaborative Framework: Sirui Hong et al., 2023, ICLR 2024 (oral). arXiv:2308.00352. https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.00352

  • Technique to borrow: Standardized Operating Procedures (SOPs) written into role prompts, in an assembly-line split where each role produces a structured intermediate artifact that the next role checks. The paper says this reduces cascading hallucination. Use it for fixed roles such as Literature Analyst, Target Assessor and Modeler, with schema-validated handoffs.

  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.00352 and https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/hash/6507b115562bb0a305f1958ccc87355a-Abstract-Conference.html

  • Also verified, optional: More Agents Is All You Need: Junyou Li et al., 2024, TMLR. arXiv:2402.05120. https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.05120

  • Technique to borrow: sampling and voting ("Agent Forest"). Sample N agent answers and take a majority vote. Gains grow with N and with task difficulty, and the method works alongside debate or CoT.
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.05120

docs.title: 5. Budget and stopping control (token, cost and latency budgets; adaptive compute)
docs.text:
• Budget-Aware Tool-Use Enables Effective Agent Scaling (BATS): Tengxiao Liu et al., 2025, arXiv preprint. arXiv:2511.17006. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.17006
  • Technique to borrow:
    • Budget Tracker: a <budget> block appended after every tool response, for example Query Budget Used/Remaining, URL Budget Used/Remaining, plus "Make the best use of the available resources". It defines tiers: HIGH at 70% or more remaining, MEDIUM 30-70%, LOW 10-30%, CRITICAL below 10%.
    • Self-verification step: labels each constraint satisfied, contradicted or unverifiable, then decides SUCCESS, CONTINUE (dig deeper) or PIVOT (on a contradiction or when budget is insufficient), and replaces the raw trajectory with a summary.
    • Unified cost: C = c_token + sum over tools of c_i * P_i.

  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/html/2511.17006v1

  • FrugalGPT: How to Use Large Language Models While Reducing Cost and Improving Performance: Lingjiao Chen et al., 2023, arXiv preprint (no venue found). arXiv:2305.05176. https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.05176

  • Technique to borrow: an LLM cascade. Query an ordered list of models. A learned scorer g(q, a) in [0, 1] (DistilBERT regression in the paper) accepts the answer at stage i if g > tau_i, otherwise the next model is called. The list and thresholds are optimized to maximize expected reward subject to expected cost staying within budget b. Example thresholds: GPT-J 0.96, J1-L 0.37, with GPT-4 as the final fallback. Reported up to 98% cost reduction at GPT-4 accuracy.

  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/html/2305.05176

  • Token-Budget-Aware LLM Reasoning (TALE): Tingxu Han et al., 2024, Findings of ACL 2025. arXiv:2412.18547. DOI 10.18653/v1/2025.findings-acl.1274. https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.18547

  • Technique to borrow: estimate a per-query token budget from the problem's complexity and state it in the prompt, for example "use less than N tokens". This shortens reasoning with a modest accuracy cost. Use it to set per-node reasoning budgets inside the plan.

  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.18547 and https://aclanthology.org/2025.findings-acl.1274/

  • Adaptive-RAG: Learning to Adapt Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models through Question Complexity: Soyeong Jeong et al., 2024, NAACL 2024. arXiv:2403.14403. https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.14403

  • Technique to borrow: a small classifier predicts query complexity and routes the query to one of three strategies: no retrieval, single-step RAG, or iterative multi-step RAG. Training labels are collected automatically. Use this as the entry gate that picks between the quick-answer path, the plan-and-execute path and the deep-research path.
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.14403

docs.title: 6. Hypothesis-to-experiment loop
docs.text:
• Towards an AI co-scientist (v1 title; v2 retitled "Accelerating scientific discovery with Co-Scientist"): Juraj Gottweis et al., 2025. arXiv:2502.18864. The arXiv comments note Nature (2026), DOI 10.1038/s41586-026-10644-y. https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.18864
  • Technique to borrow:
    • A Supervisor runs an asynchronous queue over seven agents: Generation, Reflection (peer review, optionally with web search), Ranking, Proximity (similarity graph for dedup and pairing), Evolution, Meta-review, and the Supervisor itself.
    • Ranking is an Elo tournament. New hypotheses start at Elo 1200. Top-ranked pairs get multi-turn simulated debates and lower-ranked pairs get single-turn comparisons.
    • Meta-review feedback is appended to the other agents' prompts. This gives test-time improvement without fine-tuning.

  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.18864 and https://arxiv.org/html/2502.18864v1

  • DiscoveryAgent: An AI Agent for Designing Genetic Perturbation Experiments: Yusuf Roohani et al., 2024, ICLR 2025. arXiv:2405.17631. https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.17631

  • Technique to borrow: a closed-loop experiment design.
    • Each round the prompt holds the research problem, the measurement definition, results from previous rounds and an exclusion list ("Do not include any genes from this prompt (since they're already tested)").
    • The agent returns a Reflection, a Research Plan (at most 5 sentences) and a Solution (a batch of 128 genes, or 32 for small screens). Invalid or repeated genes trigger re-prompting.
    • A critic LLM can replace genes in the batch.
    • Tools: PubMed search (summarizes the top 5 papers) and Reactome enrichment over hit genes.
    • Evaluated over 5 rounds.

  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/html/2405.17631 and https://mlanthology.org/iclr/2025/roohani2025iclr-biodiscoveryagent

  • Robin: A multi-agent system for automating scientific discovery: Ali Essam Ghareeb et al., 2025, arXiv preprint (FutureHouse). arXiv:2505.13400. https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13400

  • Technique to borrow: a lab-in-the-loop pipeline.
    • Crow, a PaperQA2-based concise literature agent, proposes 10 candidate disease mechanisms and writes assay reports, which are ranked.
    • Robin proposes 30 candidates, and Falcon, the deep-report agent, writes a report on each.
    • Ranking uses an LLM-judge pairwise tournament: full round robin up to 25 items, otherwise 300 random pairs, fitted with a Bradley-Terry-Luce model.
    • Finch, the Jupyter data-analysis agent, runs up to 10 independent analysis trajectories, and a meta-analysis forms a consensus.
    • The resulting insights seed the next hypothesis cycle.

  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/html/2505.13400

  • Large Language Models for Automated Open-domain Scientific Hypotheses Discovery: Zonglin Yang et al., 2023, Findings of ACL 2024. arXiv:2309.02726. https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.02726

  • Technique to borrow: a multi-module hypothesis generator with three feedback mechanisms that critique and refine hypotheses for validity, novelty and helpfulness (confirm in PDF). Use these as the scoring axes in the Reflection step.
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.02726

docs.title: 7. Adversarial counter-evidence and contradiction search
docs.text:
• PaperQA2 / ContraCrow, from "Language agents achieve superhuman synthesis of scientific knowledge": Skarlinski et al., 2024. arXiv:2409.13740. https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.13740
  • Technique to borrow: the ContraCrow pipeline.
    • An LLM extracts claims from each section chunk of a paper.
    • A filter LLM scores each claim 0-10 for quality and generalizability, and only claims scoring 8 or higher are kept.
    • Each claim goes to PaperQA2 with a contradiction prompt that searches the literature for opposing evidence. The answer is on an 11-point Likert scale mapped to 0-10, with "lack of evidence" scored 5.
    • A claim is flagged as contradicted at a score of 8 or higher.
    • Results: 2.34 ± 1.99 contradictions per biology paper, 70% validated by experts.

  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/html/2409.13740

  • CRITIC: Large Language Models Can Self-Correct with Tool-Interactive Critiquing: Zhibin Gou et al., 2023, ICLR 2024. arXiv:2305.11738. https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.11738

  • Technique to borrow: a verify-then-correct loop. Produce an initial output, call external tools (search, code interpreter) to check specific claims, write a critique, revise, and repeat until the critique passes or an iteration cap is reached. The paper's point is that critique grounded in external tools is what makes self-correction work.

  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.11738

  • Chain-of-Verification Reduces Hallucination in Large Language Models (CoVe): Shehzaad Dhuliawala et al., 2023, Findings of ACL 2024. arXiv:2309.11495. DOI 10.18653/v1/2024.findings-acl.212. https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.11495

  • Technique to borrow: (1) write a draft, (2) plan verification questions, (3) answer each one independently. In the factored variant the verifier cannot see the draft, which avoids copying its errors. (4) Write the final revised answer. Use step (3) with "find evidence against X" queries as the counter-evidence pass.

  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.11495 and https://aclanthology.org/2024.findings-acl.212/

  • SciFact-Open: Towards open-domain scientific claim verification: David Wadden et al., 2022, Findings of EMNLP 2022. arXiv:2210.13777. https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.13777

  • Technique to borrow: an evaluation set and label scheme for verifying claims against about 500K abstracts, with SUPPORT/REFUTE labels and rationales. Systems built on small corpora lose 15 or more F1 at this scale. Use it to benchmark the contradiction search and to model "supports only a special case" outcomes.
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.13777

docs.title: 10. Sandboxed code-execution agent for data analysis
docs.text:
• Executable Code Actions Elicit Better LLM Agents (CodeAct): Xingyao Wang et al., 2024, ICML 2024. arXiv:2402.01030. https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.01030
  • Technique to borrow: Python code as the single action space instead of JSON tool calls. The agent emits code, the interpreter runs it, and stdout or errors come back as the observation over multiple turns. The agent self-debugs from these observations. Up to 20% higher success than JSON or text actions across 17 LLMs.

  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.01030

  • Biomni: A General-Purpose Biomedical AI Agent: Kexin Huang et al., 2025, bioRxiv preprint (posted 2 Jun 2025). DOI 10.1101/2025.05.30.656746. https://doi.org/10.1101/2025.05.30.656746

  • Technique to borrow: Biomni-A1 is built on CodeAct.
    • It first writes a numbered-list plan and keeps track of progress against it.
    • A separate prompt-based LLM retriever picks the relevant subset of tools, databases and libraries, which keeps the context short.
    • It then generates code, runs it in Python, R or Bash, and feeds the observation back until it converges.
    • Biomni-E1 contains 150 tools, 105 software packages and 59 databases. Each database is wrapped as one unified query function.
    • An ablation that swaps code-based planning for ReAct chaining performs worse.

  • Verified via: bioRxiv PDF (https://cs.stanford.edu/people/jure/pubs/biomni-biorxiv25.pdf) and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40501924/

  • BixBench: a Comprehensive Benchmark for LLM-based Agents in Computational Biology: Ludovico Mitchener et al., 2025, arXiv preprint (FutureHouse). arXiv:2503.00096. https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.00096

  • Technique to borrow: the notebook-sandbox harness and the evaluation.
    • The agent runs in Docker (BixBench-env, with Python, R and Bash bioinformatics packages) and has 3 tools: edit_cell (edit and run a Jupyter cell, which reruns the notebook), list_workdir and submit_answer. R and Bash run through %%R and %%bash.
    • The benchmark has 61 capsules and 205 open-answer questions.
    • Scoring: an LLM judge grades open answers 0/1. The multiple-choice variant includes an "Insufficient information" refusal option and takes a majority vote over 5 runs.

  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/html/2503.00096

  • Data Interpreter: An LLM Agent For Data Science: Sirui Hong et al., 2024, arXiv preprint. arXiv:2402.18679. https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.18679

  • Technique to borrow: hierarchical graph modeling. A data-science task becomes a task graph of subproblems that is refined as dependencies change. Programmable node generation refines and verifies the code for each node. Reported results: InfiAgent-DABench 75.9% to 94.9%. A good fit for multi-step Scanpy pipelines.
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.18679

docs.title: 15. Human-in-the-loop (clarifying questions, plan approval)
docs.text:
• CLAM: Selective Clarification for Ambiguous Questions with Generative Language Models: Lorenz Kuhn et al., 2022, arXiv preprint. arXiv:2212.07769. https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.07769
  • Technique to borrow: a selective clarification pipeline. (1) Prompt the LLM to decide whether the question is ambiguous. (2) Only if it is, generate a clarifying question for the user. (3) Answer using the clarified question.

  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.07769

  • Clarify When Necessary: Resolving Ambiguity Through Interaction with LMs: Michael J.Q. Zhang and Eunsol Choi, 2023, Findings of NAACL 2025 (pp. 5526-5543, per a citing paper and the author page). arXiv:2311.09469. https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.09469

  • Technique to borrow: INTENT-SIM. Simulate several plausible user intents for the query, estimate the entropy over those intents, and ask for clarification only when entropy is high. With clarification limited to 10% of examples, it roughly doubles the gain of random selection. This gives a principled threshold for when to ask.

  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.09469 and https://www.cs.utexas.edu/~mjqzhang/

  • Asking Clarifying Questions in Open-Domain Information-Seeking Conversations: Mohammad Aliannejadi et al., 2019, SIGIR 2019. arXiv:1907.06554. DOI 10.1145/3331184.3331265. https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.06554

  • Technique to borrow: a three-stage pipeline: question retrieval (candidate clarifying questions), question selection (conditioned on the query and earlier Q/A turns), then document retrieval using the answers. Use it to pick from a curated bank of biomedical clarifiers (species, tissue, disease subtype, endpoint).

  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.06554

  • Magentic-UI: Towards Human-in-the-loop Agentic Systems: Hussein Mozannar et al., 2025, arXiv preprint (Microsoft Research). arXiv:2507.22358. https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.22358

  • Technique to borrow:
    • Co-planning: the user edits the plan in a plan editor, or gives text feedback, before anything runs.
    • Action guards: the system asks for approval before potentially irreversible actions, and the user sets how often it asks.
    • Also co-tasking, multi-tasking and long-term memory. The paper says there are six mechanisms; only these five were confirmed on the abstract page.
    • It builds on Magentic-One and AutoGen.
  • This is the direct template for plan approval before expensive COPASI or Scanpy runs.
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.22358

docs.title: Venue notes
docs.text:
• arXiv-only, no peer-reviewed venue found: ReWOO, CRAG, PaperQA2, Magentic-One, Magentic-UI, FrugalGPT, BATS, Robin, BixBench, Data Interpreter, CLAM.
  • bioRxiv preprint: Biomni.
  • AI co-scientist: the arXiv comments field cites Nature (2026) and gives a related DOI. The Nature page itself was not opened.

docs.title: Tribos agentic features: verified literature and API references (Verification, Memory, Tools, Data sources)
docs.text: How I checked: titles, first authors, years and venues come from arXiv abstract pages, Crossref DOI metadata (api.crossref.org) or the venue's proceedings pages. I called the REST endpoints with curl on 2026-10-16 and the result of each call is noted. Anything I could not confirm is labelled UNVERIFIED or left out. The "technique we borrow" lines are design notes based on the papers and docs.

docs.title: 8. Semantic claim verification with NLI
docs.text:
• Fact or Fiction: Verifying Scientific Claims. Wadden, D. et al., 2020, EMNLP 2020. arXiv:2004.14974; DOI 10.18653/v1/2020.emnlp-main.609. https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.14974
  • Borrow: the SciFact task setup. For each (claim, abstract) pair, first pick rationale sentences, then predict a label in {SUPPORTS, REFUTES, NOINFO}. We use the same three labels for each claim and keep the rationale sentence IDs as evidence pointers. The dataset is at github.com/allenai/scifact.
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.14974
  • MultiVerS: Improving scientific claim verification with weak supervision and full-document context. Wadden, D. et al., submitted 2021, published 2022, Findings of NAACL 2022. arXiv:2112.01640. https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.01640
  • Borrow: one Longformer model sees the whole abstract and predicts the label and the rationale together (multitask). We pass full EuropePMC abstracts and do not split them into sentences first. It can be weakly supervised on abstracts that have no rationale annotations.
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.01640
  • FActScore: Fine-grained Atomic Evaluation of Factual Precision in Long Form Text Generation. Min, S. et al., 2023, EMNLP 2023 (main). arXiv:2305.14251. https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14251
  • Borrow: split each answer into atomic facts with an LLM. Check each fact against retrieved passages. Score = the fraction of atomic facts that are supported. We use this as the per-answer "verified fraction" metric.
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14251
  • AlignScore: Evaluating Factual Consistency with a Unified Alignment Function. Zha, Y. et al., 2023, ACL 2023. arXiv:2305.16739. https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.16739
  • Borrow: a RoBERTa "alignment" function trained on many tasks. Split the context into chunks and the claim into sentences. For each claim sentence take the best-matching chunk, then average across sentences.
  • CPU checkpoints: HF yzha/AlignScore, files AlignScore-base.ckpt (RoBERTa-base, about 125M) and AlignScore-large.ckpt (RoBERTa-large, about 355M). MIT licence.
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.16739 and https://huggingface.co/yzha/AlignScore
  • MiniCheck: Efficient Fact-Checking of LLMs on Grounding Documents. Tang, L. et al., 2024, EMNLP 2024. arXiv:2404.10774. https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.10774
  • Borrow: a small checker that labels each (document, sentence) pair as supported (1) or unsupported (0) and also returns a probability. Long documents are split into chunks and the maximum chunk score is taken. The model card gives no recommended threshold, so we must calibrate one ourselves (see feature 9).
  • CPU checkpoints (HF): lytang/MiniCheck-RoBERTa-Large (0.4B), lytang/MiniCheck-DeBERTa-v3-Large (0.4B), lytang/MiniCheck-Flan-T5-Large (base google/flan-t5-large, under 1B, MIT). The larger option is bespokelabs/Bespoke-MiniCheck-7B (7B, GPU).
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.10774 and https://huggingface.co/lytang/MiniCheck-Flan-T5-Large
  • SummaC: Re-Visiting NLI-based Models for Inconsistency Detection in Summarization. Laban, P. et al., submitted 2021, published 2022, TACL. arXiv:2111.09525. https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.09525
  • Borrow: run NLI at sentence level. Build a matrix of entailment scores (source sentences × claim sentences). SummaC-ZS takes the maximum over source sentences for each claim sentence, then averages over claim sentences. SummaC-Conv learns a 1-D convolution over a histogram of the scores. This is the zero-shot baseline we can run with any NLI cross-encoder.
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.09525
  • Generic NLI cross-encoder (not a paper, model card only): HF cross-encoder/nli-deberta-v3-base. Trained on SNLI and MultiNLI, Apache-2.0. Output label order is 0 = contradiction, 1 = entailment, 2 = neutral. Hard-code this mapping in the code, because other NLI models order their labels differently. The model card does not mention xsmall, small or large siblings, so check those IDs before using them.
  • Verified via: https://huggingface.co/cross-encoder/nli-deberta-v3-base

docs.title: 9. Calibrated per-claim confidence
docs.text:
• Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know. Kadavath, S. et al., 2022, arXiv preprint (Anthropic). arXiv:2207.05221. https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.05221
  • Borrow: self-evaluation with P(True). The model proposes an answer, then is asked whether the answer is True or False, and we read the probability of "True" as the confidence. The paper also trains a P(IK) ("I know") head.
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.05221
  • Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? An Empirical Evaluation of Confidence Elicitation in LLMs. Xiong, M. et al., 2023, ICLR 2024. arXiv:2306.13063. https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.13063
  • Borrow: a three-part recipe of prompting for a stated confidence, sampling several answers, and combining them by consistency. Report ECE and AUROC. We use the stated confidence combined with sample agreement where we can only reach the LLM through an API (NIM) and have no logits.
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.13063
  • Detecting hallucinations in large language models using semantic entropy. Farquhar, S. et al., 2024, Nature 630(8017):625–630. DOI 10.1038/s41586-024-07421-0. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07421-0
  • Borrow: sample N answers and group them into meaning clusters using bidirectional entailment (A entails B and B entails A, judged by an NLI model or LLM). Compute the entropy over the clusters. High entropy flags a likely confabulation. We can reuse the feature-8 NLI cross-encoder for the clustering.
  • Verified via: https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1038/s41586-024-07421-0
  • On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks. Guo, C. et al., 2017, ICML 2017. arXiv:1706.04599. https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.04599
  • Borrow: temperature scaling, which fits one scalar T on a held-out set by minimising NLL and then uses softmax(z/T). Measure with ECE (equal-width bins) and reliability diagrams. We apply it to the logits from the NLI/MiniCheck verifier.
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.04599
  • Conformal Language Modeling. Quach, V. et al., 2023, ICLR 2024. arXiv:2306.10193. https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.10193
  • Borrow: sample candidates, reject low-quality ones, and stop once a calibrated rule is met, so that the returned set contains an acceptable answer with probability at least 1−ε. It can also pick out individual components (sentences) that are confidently correct.
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.10193
  • Language Models with Conformal Factuality Guarantees. Mohri, C. & Hashimoto, T., 2024, ICML 2024, PMLR 235:36029–36047. arXiv:2402.10978. https://proceedings.mlr.press/v235/mohri24a.html
  • Borrow: split the output into sub-claims and score each one. Compute a split-conformal threshold on a calibration set, then drop sub-claims below it ("back-off"). This gives a guarantee that the remaining text is correct with probability at least 1−α (80–90% in the paper). This matches our per-claim pipeline from feature 8.
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.10978 and https://proceedings.mlr.press/v235/mohri24a.html

docs.title: 11. SBML model calibration, parameter estimation and identifiability
docs.text:
• COPASI—a COmplex PAthway SImulator. Hoops, S. et al., 2006, Bioinformatics 22(24):3067–3074. DOI 10.1093/bioinformatics/btl485. https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btl485
  • Borrow: COPASI's parameter-estimation task, with its choice of local and global optimisers (e.g. Levenberg–Marquardt, particle swarm, evolutionary programming), and its sensitivity tasks. We drive these through basico.
  • Verified via: https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1093/bioinformatics/btl485
  • BASICO: A simplified Python interface to COPASI. Bergmann, F. T. et al., 2023, Journal of Open Source Software 8(90):5553. DOI 10.21105/joss.05553. https://doi.org/10.21105/joss.05553
  • Borrow (functions confirmed in the basico API docs): load_biomodel, run_time_course, get_parameters. From basico.task_parameterestimation: add_experiment, set_fit_parameters, run_parameter_estimation, get_fit_statistic, get_parameters_solution. From basico.task_sensitivities: run_sensitivities. I found no built-in profile-likelihood helper in basico. Use pyPESTO for profiles, or write a loop that fixes one parameter at a time and re-runs run_parameter_estimation.
  • Verified via: https://api.crossref.org/works/10.21105/joss.05553 and https://basico.readthedocs.io/en/latest/API/basico.html
  • Structural and practical identifiability analysis of partially observed dynamical models by exploiting the profile likelihood. Raue, A. et al., 2009, Bioinformatics 25(15):1923–1929. DOI 10.1093/bioinformatics/btp358. https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btp358
  • Borrow: the profile likelihood PL(θ_i) = min over θ_{j≠i} of χ²(θ). The confidence interval is where PL rises less than the χ²(α, df) quantile above the optimum (3.84 for a pointwise 95% interval with df = 1). A profile that stays flat means the parameter is structurally non-identifiable. A profile that is open on one side means it is practically non-identifiable.
  • Verified via: https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1093/bioinformatics/btp358
  • pyPESTO: a modular and scalable tool for parameter estimation for dynamic models. Schälte, Y. et al., 2023, Bioinformatics 39(11):btad711. DOI 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad711. https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btad711
  • Borrow: multi-start optimisation, the pypesto.profile module for profiles, sampling for posterior uncertainty, and the PEtab problem format. Use it if we export the basico problem to PEtab.
  • Verified via: https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1093/bioinformatics/btad711
  • Benchmark problems for dynamic modeling of intracellular processes. Hass, H. et al. (with Kreutz, C.), 2019, Bioinformatics 35(17):3073–3082. DOI 10.1093/bioinformatics/btz020. https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btz020
  • Borrow: a set of curated ODE models with real data, which we use as regression tests for the calibration agent (does our pipeline recover published fits and identifiability results?).
  • Verified via: https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1093/bioinformatics/btz020

docs.title: 12. Structure and chemistry agents
docs.text:
• Highly accurate protein structure prediction with AlphaFold. Jumper, J. et al., 2021, Nature 596(7873):583–589. DOI 10.1038/s41586-021-03819-2. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-021-03819-2
  • Borrow: per-residue confidence pLDDT (0–100, with bands below 50, 50–70, 70–90 and above 90) and PAE. The agent should report both alongside any structure-based claim.
  • Verified via: https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1038/s41586-021-03819-2
  • AlphaFold Protein Structure Database: massively expanding the structural coverage of protein-sequence space with high-accuracy models. Varadi, M. et al., 2022 (online Nov 2021), Nucleic Acids Res. 50(D1):D439–D444. DOI 10.1093/nar/gkab1061.
  • Verified via: https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1093/nar/gkab1061
  • AlphaFold Protein Structure Database in 2024: providing structure coverage for over 214 million protein sequences. Varadi, M. et al., 2024, Nucleic Acids Res. 52(D1):D368–D375. DOI 10.1093/nar/gkad1011.
  • API: GET https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/api/prediction/{UniProt accession}. Live check on P04637 returned 200 with a JSON array containing modelEntityId "AF-P04637-F1", toolUsed and related fields. The response also links to PDB/mmCIF/PAE files.
  • Verified via: https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1093/nar/gkad1011 and a live call to https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/api/prediction/P04637
  • Evolutionary-scale prediction of atomic-level protein structure with a language model (ESMFold / ESM-2). Lin, Z. et al., 2023, Science 379(6637):1123–1130. DOI 10.1126/science.ade2574.
  • NIM: POST https://health.api.nvidia.com/v1/biology/nvidia/esmfold. An unauthenticated call returned 401 "authorization missing", while a made-up path under the same host returned 404, so the route exists. I could not fetch an official docs page for the request schema, so the body field name is UNVERIFIED (commonly {"sequence": "..."}). Check it on build.nvidia.com/meta/esmfold before coding against it.
  • Verified via: https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1126/science.ade2574 and a live endpoint probe
  • DiffDock: Diffusion Steps, Twists, and Turns for Molecular Docking. Corso, G. et al., 2022 (arXiv), ICLR 2023. arXiv:2210.01776. https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.01776
  • Borrow: a generative docking model that ranks poses with a confidence model. NIM: POST https://health.api.nvidia.com/v1/biology/mit/diffdock (OpenAPI path /molecular-docking/diffdock/generate). It needs a Bearer NVIDIA_API_KEY. Body fields: protein (PDB text), ligand (text), ligand_file_type (mol2, sdf or txt), num_poses (default 10, max 100), time_divisions (≤20), steps (≤18), save_trajectory, skip_gen_conformer, is_staged.
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.01776 and https://docs.api.nvidia.com/nim/reference/mit-diffdock-infer (live probe returned 401)
  • Improving Small Molecule Generation using Mutual Information Machine (MolMIM). Reidenbach, D. et al., 2022 (v2 2023), MLDD workshop at ICLR 2023. arXiv:2208.09016. https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.09016
  • Borrow: generate molecules in latent space, steered by CMA-ES. NIM endpoints (self-hosted, all POST): /generate, /embedding, /hidden, /decode, /sampling. /generate takes smi (seed SMILES), algorithm ("CMA-ES" or "none"), num_molecules (1–100), property_name ("QED" or "plogP"), min_similarity (0–0.7). Hosted: POST https://health.api.nvidia.com/v1/biology/nvidia/molmim/generate (live probe returned 401, so the route exists).
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.09016 and https://docs.nvidia.com/nim/bionemo/molmim/latest/endpoints.html
  • RCSB Protein Data Bank (RCSB.org): delivery of experimentally-determined PDB structures alongside one million computed structure models of proteins from artificial intelligence/machine learning. Burley, S. K. et al., 2023, Nucleic Acids Res. 51(D1):D488–D508. DOI 10.1093/nar/gkac1077.
  • API: Data API GET https://data.rcsb.org/rest/v1/core/entry/{PDB_ID} (live 200 for 4HHB). Search API https://search.rcsb.org/rcsbsearch/v2/query?json=... (live 200 for a full_text "TP53" query).
  • Verified via: https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1093/nar/gkac1077 and live calls

docs.title: 13. Durable long-running agent jobs and living literature monitoring
docs.text:
• LangGraph Persistence (docs, not a paper). https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/persistence
  • Borrow: checkpointers that save graph state for each thread_id, passed as {"configurable": {"thread_id": ...}}. Options are InMemorySaver (development only, lost on restart), SqliteSaver (local file) and PostgresSaver/AsyncPostgresSaver (production). thread_id must be 255 characters or fewer with Postgres. The checkpoints also support human-in-the-loop interrupts and resume. The old /durable-execution URL now loads this Persistence page (it has a #durability-modes anchor with no visible text), so cite the Persistence URL. Related page: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/checkpointers
  • Verified via: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/persistence
  • Living Systematic Reviews: An Emerging Opportunity to Narrow the Evidence-Practice Gap. Elliott, J. H. et al., 2014, PLoS Medicine 11(2):e1001603. DOI 10.1371/journal.pmed.1001603.
  • Borrow: the idea of a review that is updated continuously as new evidence is published. This justifies scheduled EuropePMC and bioRxiv re-queries that update a saved project's claims.
  • Verified via: https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1371/journal.pmed.1001603
  • Living systematic review: 1. Introduction—the why, what, when, and how. Elliott, J. H. et al., 2017, J. Clin. Epidemiol. 91:23–30. DOI 10.1016/j.jclinepi.2017.08.010.
  • Borrow: the operational rules. Search on a fixed, stated schedule (e.g. monthly). Fold new evidence in promptly. Say up front when the review is updated and when it stops being "living".
  • Verified via: https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/j.jclinepi.2017.08.010
  • I did not verify a peer-reviewed paper on durable execution for LLM agents specifically, so none is listed.

docs.title: 16. Project-level and agent memory
docs.text:
• MemGPT: Towards LLMs as Operating Systems. Packer, C. et al., 2023, arXiv. arXiv:2310.08560. https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.08560
  • Borrow: memory split into tiers like an operating system. "Main context" is the working memory inside the prompt, and archival and recall storage live outside it. The agent moves information between tiers with function calls (it "pages" memory in and out).
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.08560
  • Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior. Park, J. S. et al., 2023, UIST '23 (ACM), pp. 1–22. arXiv:2304.03442; DOI 10.1145/3586183.3606763.
  • Borrow: a memory stream ranked by a weighted sum of recency (exponential decay), importance (an LLM-rated score from 1 to 10) and relevance (embedding cosine). The agent also periodically writes "reflections" that summarise higher-level insights.
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.03442 and https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/3586183.3606763
