  • Mem0: Building Production-Ready AI Agents with Scalable Long-Term Memory. Chhikara, P. et al., 2025, arXiv. arXiv:2504.19413. https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.19413
  • Borrow: an extract-then-update loop. Pull candidate memories out of each exchange, then have an LLM choose ADD, UPDATE, DELETE or NOOP against similar existing memories. There is also a graph variant.
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.19413
  • Zep: A Temporal Knowledge Graph Architecture for Agent Memory. Rasmussen, P. et al., 2025, arXiv. arXiv:2501.13956. https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.13956
  • Borrow: Graphiti's bi-temporal edges. Each fact records when it was true and when it was ingested. When a new fact contradicts an old one, the old fact is marked invalid rather than deleted. This suits project memory where findings get revised over time.
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.13956
  • HippoRAG: Neurobiologically Inspired Long-Term Memory for Large Language Models. Gutiérrez, B. J. et al., 2024, NeurIPS 2024. arXiv:2405.14831. https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14831
  • Borrow: an LLM extracts an open knowledge graph, and Personalized PageRank is run from the entities in the query to retrieve across multiple hops. This fits well with our PrimeKG graph.
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14831
  • A-MEM: Agentic Memory for LLM Agents. Xu, W. et al., 2025, NeurIPS 2025. arXiv:2502.12110. https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.12110
  • Borrow: memory notes in the Zettelkasten style, each with keywords, tags and links. The links are created and updated by the LLM, and the notes evolve as new memories arrive.
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.12110

docs.title: 17. MCP server and agent interoperability
docs.text:
• Model Context Protocol specification (not a paper). The current version is 2026-07-28: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/
  • Note: this version uses per-request version negotiation through _meta["io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion"] and the MCP-Protocol-Version header on Streamable HTTP, plus a required server/discover RPC. Revisions 2025-11-25 and earlier use the initialize-handshake model and have a backward-compatibility section. If we pin an older SDK, cite https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/ instead.
  • Verified via: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/versioning
  • Agent2Agent (A2A) Protocol specification (not a paper). Latest released version is 1.0.0 (earlier: 0.3.0, 0.2.6, 0.1.0). The page says A2A has joined the Agentic AI Foundation. https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/specification/
  • Borrow: an Agent Card served at https://{domain}/.well-known/agent-card.json. Bindings: JSON-RPC, gRPC and HTTP+JSON/REST. Methods: SendMessage, SendStreamingMessage, GetTask, ListTasks, CancelTask, SubscribeToTask, the push-notification config CRUD methods, and GetExtendedAgentCard. In v1.0 these names are PascalCase; the older slash names such as message/send came from versions before 1.0.
  • Verified via: https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/specification/
  • Model Context Protocol (MCP): Landscape, Security Threats, and Future Research Directions. Hou, X. et al., 2025, arXiv. arXiv:2503.23278. https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.23278
  • Borrow: the paper's threat taxonomy across the MCP server lifecycle (creation, operation, update), covering risks such as tool poisoning, name collisions, and configuration drift or privilege persistence. We use it as a checklist when exposing Tribos tools as an MCP server.
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.23278

docs.title: 18. Tool retrieval and selection from a large tool catalogue
docs.text:
• ToolLLM: Facilitating Large Language Models to Master 16000+ Real-world APIs. Qin, Y. et al., 2023 (arXiv), ICLR 2024. arXiv:2307.16789. https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/hash/28e50ee5b72e90b50e7196fde8ea260e-Abstract-Conference.html
  • Borrow: a neural API retriever that picks the top-k tools for each instruction, DFSDT (depth-first search over a decision tree, which lets the agent back off from failed tool paths), and ToolEval pass/win rates.
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.16789 and the ICLR proceedings link above
  • Gorilla: Large Language Model Connected with Massive APIs. Patil, S. G. et al., 2023 (arXiv), NeurIPS 2024. arXiv:2305.15334. https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/e4c61f578ff07830f5c37378dd3ecb0d-Paper-Conference.pdf
  • Borrow: retriever-aware training, meaning the retrieved API documentation is put in the prompt so the model stays correct when the docs change. Also the AST sub-tree matching check for hallucinated API calls.
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.15334 and https://neurips.cc/virtual/2024/poster/93353
  • Democratizing AI scientists using ToolUniverse. Gao, S. et al. (with Zitnik, M.), 2025, arXiv. arXiv:2509.23426. https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.23426
  • Borrow: a standard tool specification over more than 600 biomedical tools, with "Tool Finder" retrieval, and tools that can be refined or generated from natural-language descriptions. Code is at github.com/mims-harvard/ToolUniverse. It already wraps DepMap and NVIDIA NIM tools, which we can use as a reference implementation.
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.23426v1
  • Re-Invoke: Tool Invocation Rewriting for Zero-Shot Tool Retrieval. Chen, Y. et al., 2024, Findings of EMNLP 2024. arXiv:2408.01875. https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.01875
  • Borrow: at indexing time, an LLM writes synthetic queries for each tool document. At query time, the user's intent is extracted and tools are ranked across intents. No training is needed.
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.01875
  • Toolshed: Scale Tool-Equipped Agents with Advanced RAG-Tool Fusion and Tool Knowledge Bases. Lumer, E. et al., 2024, arXiv. arXiv:2410.14594. https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.14594
  • Borrow: three stages. Before retrieval, enrich each tool document (questions, keywords). During retrieval, rewrite and expand the query. After retrieval, rerank the results.
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.14594
  • Retrieval Models Aren't Tool-Savvy: Benchmarking Tool Retrieval for Large Language Models (ToolRet). Shi, Z. et al., 2025, ACL 2025. arXiv:2503.01763. https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.01763
  • Borrow: an evaluation benchmark and method (code: github.com/mangopy/tool-retrieval-benchmark). Its finding is that generic IR embedders do badly on tool retrieval, so we should measure recall@k on our own catalogue.
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.01763

docs.title: 19. Tool reliability (retries, caching, circuit breakers)
docs.text:
• Identifying the Risks of LM Agents with an LM-Emulated Sandbox (ToolEmu). Ruan, Y. et al., 2023 (arXiv), ICLR 2024 (Spotlight). arXiv:2309.15817. https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.15817
  • Borrow: an LLM emulates tool execution, including adversarial edge cases, so the agent can be tested without calling the real API. An LLM safety evaluator scores the risk. We use this as a test harness for failure handling.
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.15817 and https://iclr.cc/virtual/2024/poster/19037
  • ToolSword: Unveiling Safety Issues of Large Language Models in Tool Learning Across Three Stages. Ye, J. et al., 2024, ACL 2024 (Long Papers). arXiv:2402.10753. https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.10753
  • Borrow: test scenarios grouped by stage. Input stage: malicious queries and jailbreaks. Execution stage: noisy misdirection and risky cues. Output stage: harmful feedback and error conflicts. Noisy or erroneous tool output is the case most relevant to our retry and validation layer.
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.10753
  • API-Bank: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Tool-Augmented LLMs. Li, M. et al., 2023, EMNLP 2023. arXiv:2304.08244. https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.08244
  • Borrow: an error taxonomy for API calls (no call, wrong API name, bad parameters, hallucinated response). Use it to label failures in our tool-call telemetry.
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.08244
  • Circuit Breaker (article, not a paper). Fowler, M., 6 March 2014. https://martinfowler.com/bliki/CircuitBreaker.html
  • Borrow: three states. Closed: calls go through and failures are counted. Open: after a failure threshold, calls fail fast. Half-open: after a timeout, one trial call is allowed; success closes the breaker and failure re-opens it. Fowler credits Michael Nygard's Release It! for popularising the pattern. I did not separately verify the book's edition or ISBN.
  • Verified via: https://martinfowler.com/bliki/CircuitBreaker.html

docs.title: 20. New data sources (paper and live REST base URL)
docs.text:
• GWAS Catalog. Sollis, E. et al., 2023, "The NHGRI-EBI GWAS Catalog: knowledgebase and deposition resource", Nucleic Acids Res. 51(D1):D977–D985, DOI 10.1093/nar/gkac1010. Newer paper: Cerezo, M. et al., 2025, "The NHGRI-EBI GWAS Catalog: standards for reusability, sustainability and diversity", Nucleic Acids Res. 53(D1):D998–D1005, DOI 10.1093/nar/gkae1070. The Cerezo record is verified from search and abstract mirrors only; I did not check it on Crossref.
  • API: use v2 only: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/gwas/rest/api/v2. The legacy https://www.ebi.ac.uk/gwas/rest/api/... now returns HTTP 410 Gone, and the docs say "V1 was retired in August 2026". The summary-statistics API has also been retired and has no replacement. Live check: GET /gwas/rest/api/v2/studies/GCST000854 returned 200. Reference: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/gwas/rest/api/v2/docs/reference. The docs also list an official GWAS Catalog MCP server.
  • Verified via: https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1093/nar/gkac1010, https://www.ebi.ac.uk/gwas/docs/programmatic-access/rest-api, and live calls
  • DepMap. Tsherniak, A. et al., 2017, "Defining a Cancer Dependency Map", Cell 170(3):564–576.e16, DOI 10.1016/j.cell.2017.06.010. Arafeh, R. et al., 2025 (online Oct 2024), "The present and future of the Cancer Dependency Map", Nat. Rev. Cancer 25(1):59–73, DOI 10.1038/s41568-024-00763-x.
  • API: https://depmap.org/portal/api/ exists, but scripted clients get a bot-verification ("DepMap — Verification") HTML page, including on /portal/api/download/files. A DepMap forum reply says all releases are published on Figshare (e.g. https://figshare.com/articles/dataset/DepMap_23Q2_Public/22765112), and Figshare has its own API. The safer plan is to download release CSVs (CRISPRGeneEffect etc.) from Figshare or the portal and cache them locally, rather than query per gene. The Sanger side, Cell Model Passports, has a separate documented JSON:API at https://api.cellmodelpassports.sanger.ac.uk (non-commercial use). Per-gene portal routes are UNVERIFIED.
  • Verified via: https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/j.cell.2017.06.010, https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1038/s41568-024-00763-x, live probe
  • GTEx. GTEx Consortium, 2020, "The GTEx Consortium atlas of genetic regulatory effects across human tissues", Science 369(6509):1318–1330, DOI 10.1126/science.aaz1776.
  • API: https://gtexportal.org/api/v2/. Live check: GET /api/v2/reference/gene?geneId=TP53 returned 200 with gencodeId ENSG00000141510.16.
  • Verified via: https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1126/science.aaz1776 and live call
  • STRING. Szklarczyk, D. et al., 2023, "The STRING database in 2023: protein–protein association networks and functional enrichment analyses for any sequenced genome of interest", Nucleic Acids Res. 51(D1):D638–D646, DOI 10.1093/nar/gkac1000. Newer paper: Szklarczyk, D. et al., 2025, "The STRING database in 2025: protein networks with directionality of regulation", Nucleic Acids Res. 53(D1):D730–D737, DOI 10.1093/nar/gkae1113.
  • API: https://string-db.org/api/{format}/{method}. Live: /api/json/version returned 12.5 (stable address https://version-12-5.string-db.org). /api/json/network?identifiers=TP53&species=9606 returned 200 with a combined score per edge. Pin the stable versioned address so results are reproducible.
  • Verified via: Crossref (both DOIs) and live calls
  • Reactome. Milacic, M. et al., 2024, "The Reactome Pathway Knowledgebase 2024", Nucleic Acids Res. 52(D1):D672–D678, DOI 10.1093/nar/gkad1025.
  • API: https://reactome.org/ContentService/. Live: /ContentService/data/database/version returned 97.
  • Verified via: https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1093/nar/gkad1025 and live call
  • DrugBank 6.0. Knox, C. et al., 2024, "DrugBank 6.0: the DrugBank Knowledgebase for 2024", Nucleic Acids Res. 52(D1):D1265–D1275, DOI 10.1093/nar/gkad976.
  • Licence: the full data and the API need a DrugBank account and licence (free academic licence for non-commercial use, paid for commercial use), so we cannot ship or redistribute DrugBank data by default. I did not re-check the licence terms page in this pass, so this is from background knowledge. Make DrugBank an opt-in, bring-your-own-key connector, and use ChEMBL and PubChem as the default sources.
  • Verified via: https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1093/nar/gkad976
  • PubChem. Kim, S. et al., 2025, "PubChem 2025 update", Nucleic Acids Res. 53(D1):D1516–D1525, DOI 10.1093/nar/gkae1059.
  • API (PUG-REST): https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/rest/pug/<domain>/<namespace>/<identifiers>/<operation>/<output>. Live: /compound/name/aspirin/property/MolecularFormula,CanonicalSMILES/JSON returned 200 with CID 2244. Implementation note: the response key is now ConnectivitySMILES, not CanonicalSMILES, so parsers must accept both names (or request SMILES / ConnectivitySMILES explicitly).
  • Verified via: https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1093/nar/gkae1059 and live call
  • bioRxiv / medRxiv API (no database paper verified). https://api.biorxiv.org/
  • Endpoints: /details/[server]/[interval]/[cursor]/[format] (30 results per page), /pubs/... (100 per page; preprint-to-published links), /publisher/..., /funder/..., /sum/..., /usage/.... The interval can be YYYY-MM-DD/YYYY-MM-DD, N (most recent N items) or Nd (last N days). Live: /details/biorxiv/2024-01-01/2024-01-02/0 returned 200 with messages[0].total. Page through results by increasing the cursor. This is the source for the living-review monitor in feature 13.
  • Verified via: https://api.biorxiv.org/ and live call

docs.title: Guardrails: prompt injection from retrieved content and the code sandbox
docs.text:
• Not What You've Signed Up For: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection. Greshake, K. et al., 2023, AISec '23 (16th ACM Workshop on AI and Security), pp. 79–90. arXiv:2302.12173; DOI 10.1145/3605764.3623985.
  • Borrow: the threat model. Any text we retrieve (abstracts, web pages, tool outputs) can carry hidden instructions. Treat all of it as data, never as instructions, especially before passing it to the code sandbox or any tool that has side effects.
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.12173 and https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/3605764.3623985
  • Defending Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks With Spotlighting. Hines, K. et al., 2024, arXiv (Microsoft). arXiv:2403.14720. https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.14720
  • Borrow: three transforms applied to untrusted text. (1) Delimiting: wrap it in markers. This is the weakest option because an attacker who knows the markers can get around them. (2) Datamarking: replace whitespace with a special token such as ˆ and tell the model that marked text is data. This cut ASR from about 50% to under 3% for summarisation on GPT-3.5. (3) Encoding: base64-encode the text. This gives the best ASR but hurts task quality on weaker models. Overall the paper reports ASR falling from over 50% to under 2%. Datamarking is cheap and model-agnostic, so it is our default.
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/html/2403.14720
  • StruQ: Defending Against Prompt Injection with Structured Queries. Chen, S. et al., 2024, USENIX Security 2025. arXiv:2402.06363. https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.06363
  • Borrow: keep the prompt and the data in separate channels, using reserved delimiter tokens that are stripped from the data, and fine-tune the model to follow instructions only from the prompt channel. Fine-tuning is out of scope for NIM models, but the front-end idea still applies: separate channels and filter reserved tokens out of retrieved text.
  • Verified via: https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.06363

docs.title: Items left out or flagged
docs.text:
• MultiVerS checkpoints on HuggingFace: I did not verify a HuggingFace model ID for them, so none is given.
  • NLI cross-encoder siblings (cross-encoder/nli-deberta-v3-xsmall, -small, -large): the base model card does not mention them, so check each ID before use.
  • ESMFold NIM request body schema: the route was confirmed with a live 401/404 comparison, but I could not load the docs page.
  • DepMap per-gene REST routes: the portal API is behind bot verification from scripted clients.
  • No peer-reviewed paper on durable execution for agents was verified. The LangGraph docs are the reference.
  • DrugBank licence details come from background knowledge and were not re-checked.

docs.title: The adaptive research loop
docs.text:
A research project in loop mode (POST /api/campaigns with mode: "loop", the default in the web app) works on a goal until it reaches a conclusion, then writes a thesis. Code: tribos/agentic/research/.

goal ─► literature review ─► charter (deliverables, hypotheses, tests as a dependency graph)
         ┌──────────────────────────── round r ────────────────────────────┐
         │ ready tests run in parallel ─► findings ledger ─► analysis ─► judge │
         └──── judge: what is settled, which tests next, concluded? ───────┘
                    │ concluded · stagnated · nothing left · safety ceiling
                    ▼
              thesis (chapter by chapter, numbers checked) ─► PDF · DOCX · Markdown · HTML · bundle

docs.title: Phases
docs.text:
Phase Module What happens Review loop.py One research job with search on and memory recall off. If it fails, the plan is made from the goal alone and the thesis says so. Charter charter.py One model call proposes deliverables, hypotheses and tests. Code validates it: every numbered part of the goal becomes a deliverable, ids are renumbered, dependency cycles are broken, and each deliverable gets at least one test. Tests runner.py compute / simulate / estimate: a CodeAct session in the sandbox, with the research time ceiling. The last cell sets result, which holds named quantities and chart series. An independent re-implementation, which never sees the first one's code, is compared quantity by quantity. prove: a written proof plus Lean 4 formalisation. literature: a cited research job. Ledger ledger.py One finding per test run: numbers, code, stdout, figures, checks and a verification tier. Judge judge.py An analysis and a judgement per round. Code accepts only what the evidence supports (see below). Thesis thesis.py Chapters are written one call each. Tables, figures, proofs, references and appendices are assembled from the ledger. Exports tribos/export/thesis.py Typeset HTML (Google Sans, KaTeX, Tribos cover), printed to PDF by headless Chromium. DOCX, Markdown, and a reproducibility bundle with code, Lean files and ledger.json.

Tests run over the dependency graph. Up to TRIBOS_RESEARCH_PARALLEL_TESTS run at once, and a test whose dependencies pass during a round starts in the same round. A failed test is retried with its error and a "use a different method" instruction up to TRIBOS_RESEARCH_TEST_RETRIES times, then marked blocked.

docs.title: Verification tiers
docs.text:
Strongest first:

  1. formal (Lean-verified)
  2. certified (every quantity an exact integer, reproduced exactly by the separate re-implementation)
  3. replicated (a separately written re-implementation, told to use a different algorithm and not shown the first code, agrees on every quantity; it is the same model unless TRIBOS_RESEARCH_REPLICATION_MODEL names a second one, and the finding records which)
  4. computed (ran once)
  5. sourced (cited)
  6. reasoned (argument only)

Every deliverable states the tier it needs. formal meets every requirement.

docs.title: The judge's evidence rules (deterministic)
docs.text:
The judge (a model) proposes; judge.apply_judgement keeps only what the ledger supports.

  • done: a deliverable is "done" only when it cites a finding that exists, passed (not disputed), meets the deliverable's tier, and comes from a test the charter planned for that deliverable (serves). A strong finding of another deliverable's test does not settle this one. Otherwise the deliverable falls back to "partial" or "open", with the reason in its note.
  • infeasible: needs a stated reason, for example "open problem".
  • hypothesis verdicts: "supported" or "refuted" needs a finding of a test planned for that hypothesis, at the sourced level or stronger (a model-written argument alone decides nothing). "Supported" may not cite a finding that refutes it. Otherwise the verdict becomes "undecided", with the reason in its note.
  • concluded: holds only when every deliverable is done or infeasible, whatever the model says.

docs.title: Checks on the written thesis
docs.text:
• Numbers: every number in a model-written chapter must appear in the evidence (ledger values, the review, the goal). A number that is the value of one ledger quantity, in a sentence that names a different quantity, is flagged as misattributed (ledger.misattributed_numbers): "the maximum stopping time is 837,799, at n = 329" is caught. A chapter with either problem gets one repair call; what remains is listed in the run record.
  • Formal proofs: a proof is "Lean-verified" only when it compiles with no sorry or admit, declares no axiom, and the kernel's own report (#print axioms, read after a per-check random marker) lists nothing beyond Lean's standard three axioms (propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound). See tribos/verify/formal/runner.py.
  • Environment: the thesis records a manifest (research/manifest.py): Tribos version and commit, Python and library versions, Lean toolchain and Mathlib revision, the research and replication models, the sandbox backend and limits, and the sources with their retrieval times. It is summarised in the run record and written to the bundle as manifest.json, together with a statement of what the automatic checks do and do not cover (the prose's reasoning is not checked).

docs.title: Stopping
docs.text:
The loop stops at the first of these: - concluded; - stagnated: TRIBOS_RESEARCH_STAGNATION_ROUNDS rounds with no deliverable newly settled, no hypothesis newly decided and no new finding at replicated or stronger; - nothing left to run; - a safety ceiling: TRIBOS_RESEARCH_MAX_ROUNDS, TRIBOS_RESEARCH_MAX_HOURS or TRIBOS_RESEARCH_MAX_TEST_RUNS.

The ceilings are production guards; projects normally stop on the first two. The hours ceiling counts active time (loop.active_s): hours a project sat paused, after an outage or a Stop, do not count. The app and the thesis cover show that active time. The stop reason is shown in the app and printed in the thesis. Continue research turns an instruction into a new deliverable, plans tests for it and runs the loop again.

docs.title: Time estimate
docs.text: estimate.py: the remaining tests, spread over the parallel lanes, plus analysis, judging and the thesis. Test durations come from medians measured on this project's tests, then other projects' tests, then priors. Before the plan exists the estimate is labelled rough (POST /api/campaigns/estimate).

docs.title: Model-service outages
docs.text:
Research model calls retry transient provider failures (dropped connection, timeout, rate limit, 5xx) with backoff: 5 s, 20 s, then 60 s. If the service stays unreachable, the project pauses, with a resumable error, instead of recording a wrong result: - a test that failed only for that reason keeps its retries and is not blocked; - a round whose judge could not be reached stays open.

On Resume: - tests blocked by an outage run again; - a proof whose Lean check said nothing about the proof gets another formal attempt, at most two. This covers a check cut off by an outage and one where Lean could not load its library.

Before every Lean check, imports of Mathlib modules that the installed Mathlib does not have are removed, and the check records which ones (dropped_imports). An example is Mathlib.Tactic.Omega: omega is now part of Lean core. Otherwise Lean fails to load a file that does not exist, which reads like a broken installation and is never repaired.

The thesis is never written over a broken judgement.

docs.title: Isolation and durability
docs.text:
• No memory: research jobs run with recall_memory=False and persist_memory=False. A user's other conversations once leaked a Lorenz simulation into a Collatz project.
  • Durable state: the loop is a state machine over the stored campaign record. After a restart or a Stop and Resume it continues where it was; finished work is never redone.

docs.title: Accuracy tools
docs.text:
These are available to every agent, registered in tribos/extensions/axiom.py and implemented in tribos/axiom/accuracy.py:

Tool Use axiom_interval_verify Rigorous enclosure of f over a box, or a proof that f > 0 on it (or a refuting point), with a re-runnable certificate. axiom_precision_check f at 15–120 digits and in float64; flags cancellation and ill-conditioning. axiom_counterexample_search Falsifies identities, inequalities and integer properties in exact arithmetic; exhaustive on small finite domains. calcula_cross_validate Runs two independent implementations in the sandbox and compares every quantity. calcula_distribution_tests Shapiro–Wilk, D'Agostino, Anderson–Darling, KS, moments, bootstrap CIs, Q-Q points.

docs.title: API
docs.text: Route Purpose POST /api/campaigns {goal, mode: "loop"} Start a project. GET /api/campaigns/{id} The full record: charter, ledger, rounds, dashboard, estimate, activity. GET /api/campaigns/{id}/thesis?format=pdf\|docx\|md\|html\|bundle The thesis. GET /api/campaigns/{id}/files/{name} A figure. Only plain .png and .svg names inside the project's folder. POST /api/campaigns/{id}/continue {instruction} Another round of research.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default TRIBOS_RESEARCH_SANDBOX_TIMEOUT_S 300 TRIBOS_RESEARCH_MAX_ROUNDS 12 TRIBOS_RESEARCH_MAX_HOURS 8 TRIBOS_RESEARCH_MAX_TEST_RUNS 120 TRIBOS_RESEARCH_PARALLEL_TESTS 2 TRIBOS_RESEARCH_CODEACT_STEPS 10 TRIBOS_RESEARCH_TEST_RETRIES 2 TRIBOS_RESEARCH_STAGNATION_ROUNDS 2 TRIBOS_RESEARCH_CROSS_CHECK on TRIBOS_THESIS_PDF_ENGINE auto (chromium, or the fpdf fallback)

Details are in configuration.md.

docs.title: Sandbox operations runbook
docs.text: The operational companion to docs/agentic/sandbox-security.md. That page describes what the sandbox defends against and how it is built. This one covers running it: building and pinning the executor image, choosing an isolation layer, reading the degraded flag, and what to do when a limit fails.

docs.title: 1. The shape of a deployment
docs.text:
Two containers, never one:

┌───────────────────────────┐        ┌────────────────────────────────────┐
│ backend (the API)         │        │ sandbox image (the executor)       │
│                           │        │                                    │
│ holds the credentials     │        │ holds only the scientific stack    │
│ serves the API            │        │ runs model-written code            │
│ NEVER runs model code ────┼──never─▶  --network none, read-only root    │
└───────────────────────────┘        └────────────────────────────────────┘

The API process holds the API keys, the upload store and the user's sessions. It must never execute model-written code. docker/compose.yml expresses this: the backend service is hardened (read_only, tmpfs writable paths, cap_drop: [ALL], no-new-privileges, a PID limit, memory and CPU limits), and a separate sandbox-image service builds the executor image.

docker compose build sandbox-image
docker compose up -d backend web

docs.title: 2. Building and pinning the executor image
docs.text:
The image is built from docker/sandbox.Dockerfile against docker/sandbox-requirements.txt: the scientific stack only (numpy, pandas, scipy, sympy, matplotlib, h5py, pyarrow, networkx, mpmath, pint). It deliberately does not contain fastapi, uvicorn, openai, httpx, torch, transformers or langchain — the executor has no business talking to a model or an API, and a smaller image is a smaller attack surface. It has no shell tooling either (no curl, wget, git or ssh).

docker build -f docker/sandbox.Dockerfile -t tribos-sandbox:local .

Pin it by digest in production. A tag is mutable; a digest is not.

docker inspect --format='{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' tribos-sandbox:local
# tribos-sandbox@sha256:8f2c...

TRIBOS_SANDBOX_IMAGE=tribos-sandbox@sha256:8f2c...

Rebuild on a schedule (monthly is a reasonable default) to pick up upstream security fixes, and re-run the boundary gate against the new digest before promoting it:

docker build -f docker/sandbox.Dockerfile -t tribos-sandbox:staged .
TRIBOS_SANDBOX_IMAGE=tribos-sandbox:staged uv run python scripts/verify_sandbox_boundary.py

Rebuild and re-verify whenever docker/sandbox-requirements.txt, uv.lock or the Dockerfile changes. The CI sandbox-boundary job does exactly this on every change under docker/**.

docs.title: 3. Choosing the isolation layer
docs.text:
TRIBOS_SANDBOX_BACKEND selects the backend:

Value Use when Fails when container Production. The code must not share a trust domain with the host. The runtime or the image is missing: the run is refused. subprocess Local development on a machine without a container runtime. Never fails, but is not a boundary. auto The default. Container when usable, otherwise the subprocess backend. Falls back silently to the subprocess backend.

auto is a convenience, not a policy. Set TRIBOS_SANDBOX_BACKEND=container in production so that a missing runtime is a hard, visible failure instead of a quiet downgrade to an unisolated backend.

docs.title: gVisor
docs.text:
gVisor (runsc) puts a user-space kernel between the container and the host, which cuts the syscalls a compromised native extension can make. It is the single highest-value hardening step after the container itself.

docker run --runtime=runsc --rm hello-world

Configure the daemon so the sandbox images use it by default, or set the runtime per invocation. The container backend invokes the docker/podman CLI, so the runtime has to be the daemon's default rather than a per-run flag.

docs.title: nsjail
docs.text: nsjail is a namespace- and seccomp-based jail for a single process rather than a container runtime. It is a good fit when you want a boundary without a container daemon, but it needs its own integration: the container backend does not drive nsjail today. Use it behind a custom backend, not as a drop-in.

docs.title: On macOS and Windows
docs.text: Container runtimes are a Linux feature. On macOS, Docker Desktop provides them through its VM. On Windows, they need WSL2. Where no runtime is available the subprocess backend is the fallback, and the SageMath WSL mode (TRIBOS_SANDBOX_SAGE_ALLOW_WSL) is a separate concern entirely — see the security page.

docs.title: SageMath through WSL
docs.text:
On Windows, SageMath is often installed inside WSL rather than natively. That is a separate kernel: the AST policy, the environment scrub and the network guard are applied by a Python process on the Windows side, and they do not reach into WSL. The WSL SageMath path is therefore off by default, and TRIBOS_SANDBOX_SAGE_ALLOW_WSL=1 is the explicit acceptance of that risk.

Discovery follows the same rule: with the opt-in off, a WSL-only SageMath is reported as unavailable, so the tools are not offered and then refused on every call. If you turn the opt-in on, treat the WSL SageMath path as an unisolated execution path and do not expose it on a shared host.

docs.title: 4. Strict mode
docs.text:
TRIBOS_SANDBOX_STRICT_LIMITS=1

Two things change:

  1. A run whose resource limits could not be applied fails instead of continuing degraded.
  2. The subprocess backend is refused, unless TRIBOS_SANDBOX_ALLOW_UNISOLATED=1 is set explicitly. That override exists for development only; in production, treat it as a configuration error.

docs.title: 5. Reading the degraded flag
docs.text:
Every report carries the limits that actually applied:

{
  "status": "ok",
  "limits": {
    "backend": "container",
    "engine": "python",
    "timeout_s": 60,
    "memory_mb": 2048,
    "max_output_kb": 256,
    "max_disk_mb": 256,
    "max_processes": 64,
    "degraded": false,
    "degraded_reason": ""
  }
}

degraded: true means at least one limit was not applied. The usual causes:

Symptom Cause Response degraded on Windows, memory missing The Job Object could not be assigned to the child (usually a session or privilege boundary). Run the API under a job-object-capable service account, or accept the timeout and the output cap as the only bounds. In production prefer the container backend, where the limit is a cgroup limit and cannot fail this way. degraded on Linux, memory missing RLIMIT_AS was refused by the kernel or the rlimit was already lower. Check /proc/<pid>/limits. The container backend makes this moot: the memory limit there is a cgroup limit. degraded, max_processes missing RLIMIT_NPROC is per-uid, so it counts every process of the uid, not just the sandbox's. Expected when the API and the sandbox share a uid. The container backend's --pids-limit is per-container.

Alert on degraded: true. A degraded run is still bounded by the timeout, the output cap and the process-tree kill, but a memory or process cap that did not apply is a real gap.

The gateway log line carries the same information:

Sandbox execution: engine=python backend=container status=ok seconds=1.204 timeout_s=60 memory_mb=2048

It never carries the code and never carries a secret.

docs.title: 6. When a limit fails
docs.text:
The order of response, from cheapest to most drastic:

  1. A single run reports degraded. Nothing to do for one run; check the table above. If it recurs across runs, the deployment is misconfigured — fix it before it becomes a pattern.
  2. Runs start hitting the timeout. Check whether the workload really needs longer (TRIBOS_SANDBOX_TIMEOUT_S, max 110 s) or whether the model is looping. The analyst phase has a bounded loop of its own; a timeout storm usually means the model's plan is not converging, not that the limit is too tight.
  3. The memory cap trips repeatedly. Raise TRIBOS_SANDBOX_MEMORY_MB for a specific workload, but check first whether the code is loading a whole dataset into a DataFrame when it could stream it. The dataset preview is already row- and column-bounded.
  4. The disk budget trips. The write budget is real: the code is producing more than it should. Raise TRIBOS_SANDBOX_MAX_DISK_MB only with a reason.
  5. The concurrency ceiling is hit. TRIBOS_SANDBOX_MAX_CONCURRENCY (default 2) bounds how many runs may be in flight; the next one reports busy rather than queueing without bound. Raise it if the host has the memory for it: each concurrent run can take the full TRIBOS_SANDBOX_MEMORY_MB.

The container backend enforces the memory, disk and process limits in the kernel, so those cannot be "failed" the way an in-process setrlimit can — the container simply dies, and the report says the run ended without a result.

docs.title: 7. The release gate
docs.text:
docker build -f docker/sandbox.Dockerfile -t tribos-sandbox:local .
uv run python scripts/verify_sandbox_boundary.py

Exit codes:

Code Meaning 0 The boundary held. Every check passed. 1 The boundary did not hold. The output names the check that failed. 2 The boundary could not be verified (no container runtime, or the image is missing).

Run it before every release that changes the image, the Dockerfile, the requirements, the bootstrap or the container backend. Exit code 2 must fail a CI job that requires the gate — a missing runtime is not a pass.

docs.title: 8. Routine checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] TRIBOS_SANDBOX_BACKEND=container in production.
  • [ ] TRIBOS_SANDBOX_IMAGE pinned by digest.
  • [ ] TRIBOS_SANDBOX_STRICT_LIMITS=1, and TRIBOS_SANDBOX_ALLOW_UNISOLATED unset.
  • [ ] The API service has no route to the executor's writable paths, and the executor has no credentials.
  • [ ] verify_sandbox_boundary.py runs in CI and exits 0.
  • [ ] Alerts on degraded: true.
  • [ ] The image is rebuilt and re-verified on a schedule.
  • [ ] TRIBOS_SANDBOX_SAGE_ALLOW_WSL=off unless the WSL SageMath path is deliberately wanted.

docs.title: Sandboxed code analysis: threat model, architecture and configuration
docs.text:
Feature 10 lets an agent write Python and run it over a dataset the researcher attached (CodeAct, Wang et al., ICML 2024, arXiv:2402.01030; Biomni, doi:10.1101/2025.05.30.656746; BixBench, arXiv:2503.00096; Data Interpreter, arXiv:2402.18679). This page explains what the sandbox defends against, what it does not, how it is put together, and how to run it in production.

Code:

Module Role tribos/agentic/sandbox/gateway.py The single entry point. Permission, policy, limits, backend selection, audit. tribos/agentic/sandbox/backends.py The backend protocol and the ExecutionRequest / report contract. tribos/agentic/sandbox/policy.py The AST policy, with the analysis and sage profiles. tribos/agentic/sandbox/runner.py The subprocess backend: bootstrap, runtime guards, resource limits. tribos/agentic/sandbox/process.py Shared primitives: process-tree kill, environment allowlist, capped reads. tribos/agentic/sandbox/container.py The container backend (Docker / Podman): the OS-level boundary. tribos/agentic/sandbox/__init__.py Settings accessors, the request-permission context variable, dataset scoping. tribos/axiom/sagemath.py The SageMath runner, contained by the same policy and limits. tribos/agentic/analyst.py The CodeAct phase, now routed through the gateway. tribos/extensions/sandbox.py, tribos/extensions/axiom.py The registry tools (analysis_run_python, calcula_run_python, axiom_sagemath, …).

docs.title: Threat model
docs.text:
The code is untrusted even though our own model writes it. The model reads text it did not write: the question, column names and cell values of the uploaded file, earlier tool output, and retrieved papers and web pages. Any of these can carry instructions aimed at the model. This is indirect prompt injection (Greshake et al. 2023, AISec '23, arXiv:2302.12173). An injected instruction could ask the model to write code that reads secrets, calls out to the network, or reads another user's files.

Assets we protect: - server secrets: API keys and tokens in the process environment; - other users' uploads, and anything else on the server's disk; - the network position of the server (no outbound calls from analysis code); - the availability of the API process (no runaway CPU, memory, disk or output).

Out of scope: the integrity of the analysis itself. Code can compute a wrong number, and the model can misread it. That risk is handled by showing the code, its output and the dataset with the answer, by the verifier, and by allowing "insufficient information" as an answer.

docs.title: The invariant
docs.text:
Model-written code never runs in the API process, and every run passes one decision point.

That is the whole design. The API container holds the credentials; it never executes model-written code. The execution paths (analyst phase, planner DAG, direct registry calls, SageMath) all call tribos.agentic.sandbox.gateway.execute(). There is no second, unguarded way in: the gateway owns the decision "may this run?", and a backend is only reached after it says yes.

The gateway decides, in this order:

  1. Permission. The server-wide switch (TRIBOS_SANDBOX) and the per-request switch (the "Allow code analysis on datasets" option) must both allow execution. When either forbids it, no backend is called and the report says why (disabled or forbidden).
  2. Policy. The AST policy (policy.py) rejects the code before anything runs, against the engine's profile.
  3. Limits. The effective timeout, memory, output, disk and process caps are resolved from the caller's request and the server's settings. A caller may only lower a limit, never raise it.
  4. Backend selection. auto, subprocess or container (see Backend modes).
  5. Audit. One structured log line per execution: engine, backend, status, duration and the effective limits. Never the code, never a secret.

The request-level permission travels in a contextvars.ContextVar (tribos.agentic.sandbox.execution_permitted), which propagates into the asyncio.to_thread workers the registry tools run in — exactly like the existing dataset bound_scope. That is what makes the per-request toggle authoritative for direct tool calls that never went through the planner.

docs.title: The layers
docs.text:
Inside the child, the layers below still apply. None of them is a security boundary on its own. A Python process with numpy, pandas and scipy loaded has a very large attack surface, and pure-Python sandboxes have a long history of escapes. They are defence in depth underneath the container boundary, not a substitute for it.

  1. Spotlighting of untrusted text (Hines et al. 2024, arXiv:2403.14720). The dataset preview, previous outputs and the question reach the model inside <untrusted_data> blocks, with instruction-like spans neutralised (tribos/agentic/guardrails.py). The system prompt says this text is data.
  2. AST policy (policy.py), applied before anything runs:
  3. an import allowlist: numpy, pandas, scipy, sklearn, matplotlib, anndata, scanpy, statsmodels (if installed), math, statistics, json, re, collections, itertools, functools, typing, datetime;
  4. banned names, and the same names as attributes (pandas.io.common.os): os, sys, subprocess, socket, shutil, ctypes, importlib, builtins, pickle, marshal, pathlib;
  5. banned calls: eval, exec, compile, __import__, globals, locals, vars, setattr, delattr, breakpoint, input; getattr and hasattr only with a plain, non-dunder string literal;
  6. any name or attribute starting with __, frame, generator and traceback internals (gi_frame, f_globals, tb_frame, ...), and format strings that reach dunders;
  7. open() only in read mode, on a relative path inside the work directory (the input files, by name);
  8. file writers (to_csv, savefig, np.save, write_h5ad, ...) only to a literal relative path inside the work directory, never over an input file;
  9. pickle-based I/O (read_pickle, to_pickle, allow_pickle=True), which runs code on load.
  10. submodules that load native code, compile or launch programs, whatever the import spelling (BANNED_MODULES: numpy.ctypeslib, numpy.f2py, sympy.utilities.autowrap, sympy.printing.preview, the pandas clipboard, ...), and the matching names and attributes (load_library, CDLL, ctypes, autowrap, preview, Popen, startfile, the HDF5 low-level h5f API, ...). The 2026-11-04 audit (AUDIT-102) loaded kernel32 through import numpy.ctypeslib as c with a computed library name.
  11. A separate process. sys.executable -I (isolated mode: PYTHON* variables ignored, no user site-packages, the script directory not on sys.path). -S is not used because the scientific stack lives in site-packages. The working directory is a fresh temporary work/ folder that holds only read-only copies of the attached files. The bootstrap, code and output files live in a sibling folder the code cannot name (the policy rejects ..). Everything is deleted afterwards.
  12. Runtime guards in the child, installed by the bootstrap before user code runs: user code executes with a restricted builtins dict. That dict has an __import__ that re-checks the allowlist, a read-only open() confined to the work directory (this catches computed paths the AST cannot see), a getattr that refuses dunder and banned names, and no eval, exec, compile, vars or globals. stdout and stderr are capped. Two further guards close the escapes the audit found: no program can be started (subprocess.Popen, os.system/popen/spawn*/exec*/startfile, _winapi.CreateProcess and _posixsubprocess.fork_exec raise; matplotlib's animation writers once launched a configurable executable), and HDF5 opens files only inside the work directory (h5py's C-level h5f.create/h5f.open, which h5py.File calls, check the path; h5py.File(<computed path>, 'w') once created a file outside it). tests/test_fix_audit_102_sandbox_escapes.py replays the audit's payloads.
  13. No secrets in the environment. The child's environment is built from an allowlist: PATH, SYSTEMROOT/WINDIR, PATHEXT, TEMP/TMP (pointing into the run's own temp folder), PYTHONHASHSEED, and the thread and backend settings the runner sets itself (MPLBACKEND=Agg, MPLCONFIGDIR, NUMBA_CACHE_DIR, *_NUM_THREADS=1). API keys and tokens are never copied. tests/test_feat_sandbox_runtime.py checks this.
  14. No network. Before user code runs, socket.socket is replaced by a subclass whose constructor raises, and create_connection, getaddrinfo, gethostbyname and related functions raise PermissionError. This is a monkeypatch inside the interpreter, and it is the weakest layer. Native extensions that open sockets themselves are not covered. In the container backend the network is also cut at the OS level (--network none), which is what actually holds.
  15. Limits. A wall-clock timeout (default 60 s) kills the whole process tree (taskkill /T on Windows, the process group on POSIX, SIGTERM then SIGKILL on POSIX). On POSIX the bootstrap sets RLIMIT_AS (default 2048 MB), RLIMIT_CPU, RLIMIT_NOFILE, RLIMIT_FSIZE and RLIMIT_NPROC. On Windows it assigns itself to a Job Object with a per-process memory limit, a CPU-time limit and an active-process limit of TRIBOS_SANDBOX_MAX_PROCESSES (default 64) — so the code may start workers of its own, up to that ceiling. This step is best effort: if it fails the run continues with only the timeout, and the report says so (see Degraded mode). Output is capped (256 KB stdout by default, 6 figures).
  16. Dataset scoping. The model never names a path. The analyst phase binds a scope that holds the run's user id and the ids of the datasets attached to this question. The tool resolves the requested ids through DatasetStore.resolve_for_user for that user only, checks that each path lies under the upload root, and copies the files in. A call with no bound scope reads no files. The planner cannot use the tool to reach another user's upload or a server path.
  17. On by default, but never implicit. TRIBOS_SANDBOX defaults to on. When it is off, every model-written execution path is closed: the tools are not registered, the gateway returns disabled, and direct calls refuse. The per-request "Allow code analysis on datasets" option is the narrower switch: with it off, that request cannot run Python or SageMath at all, whatever the planner asks for.

docs.title: The SageMath path
docs.text:
Under strict isolation (TRIBOS_SANDBOX_STRICT_LIMITS=1) SageMath is refused unless TRIBOS_SANDBOX_ALLOW_UNISOLATED=1, like the subprocess backend: the container backend does not carry it (AUDIT-103).

SageMath used to bypass the sandbox entirely: model-written Sage ran through a bare subprocess.run with no policy, no network block, no resource caps and a timeout that did not kill descendants. It is now contained:

  • the same gateway owns it (execute(code, engine="sage"));
  • the AST policy runs with the sage profile, which widens the allowed module roots to include sage and sagemath and nothing else — the banned names, the dunder ban and the write restrictions are identical;
  • the child runs in its own process group / Job Object with the memory, CPU, process and output caps applied;
  • the socket and DNS guard is prepended to the submitted code, before the model's own code;
  • the environment is an allowlist, and HOME points at the sandbox's scratch directory — never the server user's home, which holds the credentials;
  • TRIBOS_SANDBOX_SAGE_ENABLED=off removes the tools entirely, and TRIBOS_SANDBOX=off overrides it;
  • the Sage registry entries carry the executes_code capability tag, so approval, planner filtering and the request-level toggle treat them as code execution by tag, not by name;
  • WSL mode is off by default (TRIBOS_SANDBOX_SAGE_ALLOW_WSL=on to opt in): WSL is a separate kernel, so the Python-level guards do not reach into it. Discovery and execution agree: a SageMath that is only reachable through WSL is reported as unavailable unless the opt-in is set, so the tools are never offered and then refused on every call.

docs.title: Per-run caches, not shared ones
docs.text: Each run gets its own MPLCONFIGDIR inside its own temporary directory. A shared font cache was a cross-run poisoning path: one run could leave a file the next run read. The per-run directory is removed with the rest of the run directory.

docs.title: Backend modes
docs.text:
TRIBOS_SANDBOX_BACKEND chooses how the code runs:

Mode What it does Boundary container Runs the code in TRIBOS_SANDBOX_IMAGE via Docker or Podman. OS-level boundary. Fails closed when no runtime is available. subprocess Runs the code in a hardened child process on the host. Defence in depth only. Not a boundary against a determined attacker. auto (default) Container when a runtime and the image are available, otherwise the subprocess backend. Depends on the host.

The container backend (tribos/agentic/sandbox/container.py) starts each run with:

--network none
--read-only
--tmpfs /tmp:rw,nosuid,nodev,size=<tmp_mb>m
--tmpfs /work:rw,nosuid,nodev,size=<work_mb>m
--memory <memory_mb>m
--cpus 1.0
--pids-limit <max_processes>
--cap-drop ALL
--security-opt no-new-privileges
--user 65534:65534
--mount type=bind,src=<inputs>,dst=/inputs,readonly
--mount type=bind,src=<io>,dst=/io,readonly
--mount type=bind,src=<out>,dst=/out

The inputs are mounted read-only, so the code can read the attached files but cannot change them; the work directory is a tmpfs with a size quota, so the write budget is enforced by the kernel rather than by a check. The child runs as uid 65534 (nobody), which is not the owner of anything on the host.

The host-to-container channel is split in three, each with its own trust level:

Mount Direction Mode /inputs host → container read-only: the attached files. /io host → container read-only: the bootstrap, the config and the submitted code cell. The code cannot rewrite its own policy or its own source. /out container → host the only writable mount: the result file.

Only /out is writable by the container's uid, and it is a fresh directory inside the run's own temporary tree, removed with the run.

In auto mode the runtime probe is cached. When the subprocess backend is used because no container runtime was found, the run is still bounded by the in-process limits — but it is not an OS-level boundary, and in production it should not be relied on.

docs.title: Strict mode and degraded mode
docs.text:
• Strict mode (TRIBOS_SANDBOX_STRICT_LIMITS=1): a run whose resource limits could not be applied fails instead of continuing. It also refuses the subprocess backend unless TRIBOS_SANDBOX_ALLOW_UNISOLATED=1 is set explicitly.
  • Degraded mode: when a limit cannot be applied — a Job Object that could not be assigned, an RLIMIT that could not be set — the run continues with the limits it did get, and the report says so in report["limits"]["degraded"] (a boolean) and report["limits"]["degraded_reason"] (a string). The run is never silently unbounded: it is always at least bounded by the timeout, the output cap and the process-tree kill. Watch this flag in production; a run that reports degraded did not get every cap it asked for.

docs.title: Production setup
docs.text:
Use the container backend. Any one of these works for the isolation layer:

  • A container per run (Docker or Podman) — this is what tribos/agentic/sandbox/container.py does, with --network none, --read-only, a tmpfs work directory, the dataset mounted read-only, --memory/--cpus/ --pids-limit, --cap-drop ALL, --security-opt no-new-privileges and a non-root user. This matches the BixBench harness, which runs its agent in a Docker image.
  • gVisor (runsc) as the container runtime, which adds a user-space kernel between the code and the host.
  • firejail or bubblewrap on a single Linux host: --net=none, a private /tmp, read-only binds of the input files, and seccomp.

Keep the in-process layers as well. They give useful errors back to the model and cut the attack surface.

docker/compose.yml keeps the API and the executor separate: the backend service holds the credentials and never executes model-written code; the sandbox-image service builds the executor image. The API service itself is hardened with read_only, tmpfs writable paths, cap_drop: [ALL], no-new-privileges, a PID limit and memory/CPU limits.

See docs/agentic/sandbox-operations.md for the operational runbook: building and pinning the image, gVisor and nsjail, interpreting the degraded flag, and what to do when a limit fails.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The server-wide ceilings (all in the Code sandbox group of the settings registry, tribos/config/settings.py):

Variable Default Meaning TRIBOS_SANDBOX on Master switch. off closes every model-written execution path. TRIBOS_SANDBOX_TIMEOUT_S 60 Wall-clock limit per cell, seconds (5–110). TRIBOS_SANDBOX_MEMORY_MB 2048 Memory limit per cell, MB (256–16384). TRIBOS_SANDBOX_MAX_OUTPUT_KB 256 Cap on stdout and stderr of one run, KB (16–4096). TRIBOS_SANDBOX_MAX_DISK_MB 256 Write budget of one run, MB (16–4096). TRIBOS_SANDBOX_MAX_PROCESSES 64 Process-count cap of one run (1–512). TRIBOS_SANDBOX_MAX_CONCURRENCY 2 How many sandboxed executions may run at once (1–32). TRIBOS_SANDBOX_MAX_RESULT_BYTES 3000000 Aggregate cap on one run's result payload (result, tables, figures), bytes. TRIBOS_SANDBOX_MAX_FIGURES 6 Maximum number of Matplotlib figures captured from one run. TRIBOS_SANDBOX_BACKEND auto auto, subprocess or container. TRIBOS_SANDBOX_IMAGE tribos-sandbox:local The container image to run code in. Pin by digest in production. TRIBOS_SANDBOX_STRICT_LIMITS false Fail a run whose limits could not be applied. TRIBOS_SANDBOX_ALLOW_UNISOLATED false Allow the subprocess backend in strict mode. Development only. TRIBOS_SANDBOX_SAGE_ENABLED true Offer the SageMath tools. TRIBOS_SANDBOX=off overrides this. TRIBOS_SANDBOX_SAGE_TIMEOUT_S 120 Wall-clock limit of one SageMath execution, seconds (10–600). TRIBOS_SANDBOX_SAGE_ALLOW_WSL false Allow SageMath inside WSL, where the Python-level guards do not apply.

Plus the per-request switch:

Variable Default Meaning agent_options.enable_code_analysis true A per-request switch. When false, that request runs no server-side Python or SageMath: the planner excludes the code tools, and the gateway refuses direct calls with forbidden.

Values outside the documented range are clamped by the settings registry rather than trusted. .env.example and docs/configuration.md are generated from the same registry by scripts/gen_env_reference.py.

The analyst phase also needs an agentic framework, a CSV/TSV/h5ad attachment, and a question with analysis intent (analyse, compute, statistic, correlate, regress, differential, survival, plot, distribution, compare groups, test whether). When no model is available it does not run model-written code. Instead it runs a fixed descriptive-statistics script (describe, plus group summaries when a grouping column is obvious). That script passes the same policy.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Two gates prove the boundary from the outside, the way an attacker would try it:

docker build -f docker/sandbox.Dockerfile -t tribos-sandbox:local .
uv run python scripts/verify_sandbox_boundary.py

The script starts the real container backend against the real image and asserts: the code runs, there is no network route, no name resolution, no host filesystem read, no host secret inside the container, a minimal environment, a non-root uid, the process cap, the memory cap, the timeout, no leftover directory and no orphan process. Exit code 0 means the boundary held, 1 means it did not, and 2 means it could not be verified (no container runtime) — so a CI job that requires the gate fails rather than passing silently.

tests/test_feat_sandbox_container.py covers the same boundary in the test suite, and tests/test_feat_sandbox_limits.py, tests/test_feat_sandbox_runtime.py, tests/test_feat_sagemath_sandbox.py, tests/test_feat_execution_gateway.py and tests/test_feat_sandbox_toggle.py cover the gateway, the runtime hardening, the Sage path, the request toggle and the limits. tests/test_fix_sec.py carries the SEC-8 … SEC-15 regression ledger for the new invariants.

docs.title: Known gaps
docs.text:
• Native code in allowed packages (numpy, scipy, h5py, numba) can do anything the OS lets the process do. In the subprocess backend that is still the host's OS.
  • A library function that writes files internally, or that evaluates strings, is outside what the AST can see.
  • The SageMath backend runs in the subprocess backend; the container image does not yet carry SageMath.
  • Memory and CPU limits are best effort on Windows when the Job Object cannot be assigned. The run reports degraded in that case; strict mode turns it into a failure.

docs.title: Archivon — Scholarly Literature & Theorem Synthesis Engine
docs.text:
Tribos Literature Specialist Made by ChronoStrider Engineering

Archivon is Tribos's scholarly retrieval and evidence-grounding engine for mathematics, physics, and engineering. It executes federated retrieval across preprint servers, peer-reviewed journals, mathematical review indexes, and citation graphs, verifying research integrity and grounding factual claims with immutable identifiers.

docs.title: 1. Role & Architectural Overview
docs.text:
Archivon serves as the primary scientific literature grounding layer for Tribos, ensuring that all theoretical derivations, experimental bounds, and engineering parameters are anchored in peer-reviewed literature or established preprints.

flowchart TD
    UserQuery["Scientific Query & STEM Entities"] --> ArchivonEngine["Archivon Literature Engine"]
    ArchivonEngine --> Arxiv["arXiv API (math.*, physics.*, cs.*, eess.*)"]
    ArchivonEngine --> S2["Semantic Scholar API (Citation Graph & S2PaperId)"]
    ArchivonEngine --> OpenAlex["OpenAlex API (Works, Open Access, Topics)"]
    ArchivonEngine --> Crossref["Crossref API (DOI Resolution & Retraction Checks)"]
    ArchivonEngine --> ZbMATH["zbMATH Open API (Theorems, Reviews & Zbl IDs)"]
    ArchivonEngine --> NASA["NASA ADS API (Astrophysics & Space Science)"]

    Arxiv & S2 & OpenAlex & Crossref & ZbMATH & NASA --> Fusion["Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) & Cross-Encoder Reranker"]
    Fusion --> Integrity["Retraction & Erratum Verification"]
    Integrity --> GroundedEvidence["Claim-Level Grounded Evidence with DOIs / arXiv IDs"]

docs.title: Key Capabilities
docs.text:
1. Federated STEM Multi-Source Search: Queries arXiv, Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, Crossref, zbMATH Open, and NASA ADS concurrently with rate-limited, cached HTTP adapters and circuit breakers.
  2. STEM Entity & Concept Extraction: Identifies mathematical equations, theorem names (e.g., Navier-Stokes existence, Noether's theorem, Poincaré conjecture), physical parameters, and authors via specialized STEM tokenizers.
  3. Hybrid Dense + Lexical Reranking: Merges lexical BM25 retrieval with dense scientific embeddings (SPECTER2 / Nomic-Embed), followed by cross-encoder passage-level reranking.
  4. Claim-Level Citation Grounding: Every theoretical statement or empirical constant in synthesized responses is mapped to verified arXiv:, doi:, or zbl: identifiers.
  5. Academic Integrity & Retraction Auditing: Validates publication status against Crossref and Retraction Watch databases to flag retractions, errata, or expressions of concern.

docs.title: 3. Integration with Tribos Reasoning Pipeline
docs.text:
Archivon participates in three distinct phases of the Tribos reasoning cycle:

  1. Stage 1 Evidence Gathering: Runs concurrently with Physis physical constants lookups during initial query deconstruction to acquire mathematical theorems, experimental parameters, and peer-reviewed models.
  2. Self-RAG Gap-Driven Re-Retrieval: Triggered when downstream symbolic or numerical verification fails (e.g., Axiom identifies missing boundary conditions or Dynamis encounters an undefined coefficient), querying specific literature passages to resolve the missing constraint.
  3. ContraCrow Counter-Evidence Search: Systematically executes adversarial queries looking for boundary limits, non-existence proofs, counterexamples, or refutations of preliminary hypotheses.

docs.title: Example 1: Literature Search for Quantum Hall Effect Theorems
docs.text:
import asyncio
from tribos.archivon.engine import ArchivonEngine

async def main():
    engine = ArchivonEngine()
    results = await engine.literature_search(
        query="fractional quantum Hall effect Laughlin wave function",
        max_results=5,
        sources=["arxiv", "crossref"],
    )
    for article in results.get("articles", []):
        print(f"[{article.get('doi')}] {article.get('title')} ({article.get('year')})")

asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: Example 2: Resolving Paper Metadata and Integrity
docs.text:
import asyncio
from tribos.archivon.engine import ArchivonEngine

async def main():
    engine = ArchivonEngine()
    paper = await engine.get_paper_details("2002.01234")
    if paper.get("found"):
        print(f"Title: {paper.get('title')}")
        print(f"Retracted: {paper.get('retraction_status', {}).get('is_retracted')}")

asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: Axiom — Symbolic Mathematics, Computer Algebra & Formal Verification Engine
docs.text:
Tribos Symbolic Specialist Made by ChronoStrider Engineering

Axiom is Tribos's exact computer algebra and formal verification engine. Powered by SymPy, mpmath arbitrary-precision arithmetic, and rigorous back-substitution solvers, Axiom computes closed-form solutions, evaluates calculus operations, performs symbolic linear algebra, verifies mathematical identities, and formats equations into canonical LaTeX.

docs.title: 1. Role & Architectural Overview
docs.text:
Axiom provides infallible mathematical precision to Tribos, eliminating algebraic errors, hallucinated roots, and invalid analytical steps in scientific derivations.

flowchart TD
    DerivationRequest["Mathematical Expression / Equation System"] --> AxiomEngine["Axiom Symbolic Engine"]
    AxiomEngine --> CoreAlgebra["SymPy Core Algebra (Simplify, Factor, Expand)"]
    AxiomEngine --> EquationSolvers["Equation & System Solvers (Polynomial, Transcendental)"]
    AxiomEngine --> Calculus["Calculus Suite (Diff, Integral, Limit, Series, Sum)"]
    AxiomEngine --> ODESolver["Symbolic ODE Solver (dsolve with Boundary Conditions)"]
    AxiomEngine --> LinearAlgebra["Exact Linear Algebra (Eigenvalues, Jordan, Det, Inv)"]
    AxiomEngine --> IdentityChecker["Dual Symbolic & Numerical Identity Prover"]

    EquationSolvers & ODESolver --> BackSub["Automated Back-Substitution Verification"]
    Calculus --> MpmathCheck["Arbitrary-Precision mpmath Quadrature Verification"]
    IdentityChecker --> RandomPoints["Random Complex Sampling Test"]

    BackSub & MpmathCheck & RandomPoints --> CanonicalOutput["Canonical SymPy AST + Formatted LaTeX"]

docs.title: Key Capabilities
docs.text:
1. Exact Symbolic Computer Algebra: Computes exact rational, radical, and transcendental simplifications without floating-point truncation or round-off error.
  2. Analytical Equation & System Solving: Solves linear, polynomial, and nonlinear systems over complex (\(\mathbb{C}\)) or real (\(\mathbb{R}\)) domains, with automatic verification by back-substituting solutions into original equations.
  3. Analytical Calculus & Differential Equations: Evaluates derivatives, definite/indefinite integrals, limits, Taylor/Laurent series expansions, and closed-form ODE solutions with initial/boundary conditions.
  4. Exact Linear Algebra & Spectral Analysis: Computes exact matrix determinants, inverses, eigenvalues with algebraic/geometric multiplicities, eigenvectors, and Jordan canonical forms.
  5. Dual-Tier Identity Verification: Proves or refutes equivalence \(LHS \equiv RHS\) by checking if \(\text{simplify}(LHS - RHS) = 0\) symbolically and sampling random test points in \(\mathbb{C}\) at high numerical precision via mpmath.
  6. Canonical LaTeX Generation: Parses raw mathematical strings and outputs standardized LaTeX representations for frontend KaTeX rendering.

docs.title: 3. Integration with Tribos Reasoning Pipeline
docs.text:
• Derivation Construction: When synthesizing responses to mathematical or physical questions, Axiom provides exact steps and intermediate symbolic reductions.
  • Reflexion Verification: The TribosVerifier passes all claimed equations through axiom_verify_identity and axiom_solve to ensure no false mathematical claims survive auditing.
  • Dimensional Coordination: Works in tandem with Physis to ensure that symbolic variables in differential equations maintain physical dimensional homogeneity.

docs.title: Example 1: Solving an Initial Value Problem ODE
docs.text:
from tribos.axiom.engine import axiom_dsolve

result = axiom_dsolve(
    equation="y''(t) + 9*y(t) = 0",
    func="y(t)",
    ics={"y(0)": 2, "y'(0)": 0},
)
print("Solution:", result["solution"])  # 2*cos(3*t)
print("LaTeX:", result["latex"])        # 2 \cos{\left(3 t \right)}
assert result["verified"] is True

docs.title: Example 2: Verifying an Analytical Identity
docs.text:
from tribos.axiom.engine import axiom_verify_identity

check = axiom_verify_identity(
    lhs="1 + tan(x)^2",
    rhs="sec(x)^2",
)
assert check["equivalent"] is True
assert check["symbolic_zero"] is True

docs.title: Calcula — Sandboxed Scientific Computation & Dataset Analysis Engine
docs.text:
Tribos Computation Specialist Made by ChronoStrider Engineering

Calcula is Tribos's sandboxed scientific computing and experimental dataset analysis engine. Operating within a secure, network-isolated subprocess sandbox, Calcula executes arbitrary scientific Python code (NumPy, SciPy, SymPy, Pandas, Pint, Matplotlib, NetworkX, mpmath, and statsmodels) and automatically inspects, summarizes, and validates uploaded experimental datasets (CSV, TSV, HDF5, MAT, Parquet, XLSX).

docs.title: 1. Role & Architectural Overview
docs.text:
Calcula enables Program-Aided Language (PAL) and CodeAct execution patterns, allowing Tribos to write and execute self-contained computational scripts to perform empirical analyses, Monte Carlo simulations, signal processing, and statistical tests.

flowchart TD
    AnalysisRequest["Analytical Code or Dataset Upload"] --> SandboxManager["Calcula Sandbox Controller"]
    SandboxManager --> SecurityPolicy["Security Boundaries: Zero Network, Subprocess Sandbox, AST Filter"]
    SecurityPolicy --> PythonRunner["Isolated Python Subprocess Environment"]

    PythonRunner --> ScientificStack["NumPy, SciPy, SymPy, Pandas, Pint, Matplotlib, mpmath, statsmodels"]
    PythonRunner --> DatasetHandler["Dataset Ingestion (CSV, TSV, HDF5, MAT, Parquet)"]

    ScientificStack --> Results["Computed Variables in `result` & stdout/stderr"]
    ScientificStack --> Figures["Active Matplotlib Figures -> Base64 PNGs"]
    DatasetHandler --> Schema["Column Profiles, Summary Statistics & Outlier Metrics"]

docs.title: Key Capabilities
docs.text:
1. Subprocess Sandbox Security: Runs Python code in a sandboxed subprocess without network access, subject to memory ceilings (TRIBOS_SANDBOX_MEMORY_MB, default 1024 MB) and wall-clock execution cutoffs (TRIBOS_SANDBOX_TIMEOUT_S, default 60s).
  2. Comprehensive Scientific Software Stack: Out-of-the-box availability of NumPy, SciPy, SymPy, Pandas, Pint, Matplotlib, NetworkX, mpmath, scikit-learn, and statsmodels.
  3. Automated Dataset Profiling: Ingests uploaded data files (CSV, TSV, XLSX, Parquet, JSON, HDF5, and MAT), extracting row counts, column data types, missing value percentages, distributions, and summary statistics.
  4. Program-Aided Reasoning & Plotting: Executes custom data transforms, FFT spectral analyses, and Monte Carlo uncertainty propagations, returning open Matplotlib figures as base64-encoded PNGs.
  5. Cryptographic Provenance: Computes SHA-256 digests over code and input dataset IDs, tagging every result with an immutable canonical ID (comp:calcula_run_python:<hash>).

docs.title: calcula_run_python
docs.text:
Executes sandboxed Python computation and analysis scripts against optional attached datasets.

  • Domain: analysis
  • Adapter Type: LOCAL_COMPUTE
  • Timeout: 120.0 seconds
  • Legacy Alias: analysis_run_python

docs.title: Input Schema (AnalysisRunInput)
docs.text: Field Type Required Default Description code str Yes — Python script to execute (max 20,000 characters). Assign computed output to the result variable. dataset_ids list[str] No [] Optional attached dataset IDs (ds_<12 hex>) resolved into the script's local working directory. timeout_s int No 60 Execution cutoff in seconds (5–110s).

docs.title: Script Environment Rules
docs.text:
• Input files: Files listed in dataset_ids are mapped to local filenames matching their dataset metadata.
  • Output capture: Assign the primary return value to a global variable named result.

docs.title: 3. Integration with Tribos Reasoning Pipeline
docs.text:
• Program-Aided Verification: When an empirical verification cannot be evaluated symbolically by Axiom or analytically through Dynamis ODE presets, the agentic planner writes a self-contained Python script to verify numerical bounds.
  • Reflexion Numerical Checking: TribosVerifier verifies that numbers asserted in the final report match the result dictionary values emitted by calcula_run_python.
  • Dataset Provenance: Uploaded datasets are verified for integrity upon ingestion and cited as immutable data artifacts in final reports.

docs.title: Example 1: Monte Carlo Uncertainty Propagation in the Sandbox
docs.text:
from tribos.extensions.sandbox import run_calcula_python

script = """
import numpy as np

# Estimate uncertainty in beam deflection: delta = (F * L^3) / (3 * E * I)
n_samples = 100_000
F = np.random.normal(1000, 50, n_samples)      # Force in N
L = np.random.normal(2.0, 0.01, n_samples)     # Length in m
E = np.random.normal(200e9, 5e9, n_samples)    # Modulus in Pa
I = np.random.normal(1e-5, 1e-7, n_samples)    # Moment of inertia in m^4

delta = (F * L**3) / (3 * E * I)

result = {
    "mean_deflection_mm": float(np.mean(delta) * 1e3),
    "std_deflection_mm": float(np.std(delta) * 1e3),
    "p95_deflection_mm": float(np.percentile(delta, 95) * 1e3),
}
"""

out = run_calcula_python(code=script)
print("Deflection summary:", out.data["result"])
assert out.success is True

docs.title: Zero-Docker Cloud Architecture & Deployment Guide — Tribos
docs.text:
Tribos — Biomedical Research Assistant Made by ChronoStrider Engineering

This guide describes how to configure, run, and deploy Tribos (engineered by ChronoStrider Engineering / ChronoStrider Engineering) with zero Docker dependencies, using a 100% cloud-native architecture powered by BioContext MCP.

docs.title: 🌟 Architectural Principles
docs.text:
1. Zero Docker Dependency:
  2. No local containers required (no docker compose up, no etcd, no minio, no milvus-standalone).
  3. Run directly with uv on any workstation, cloud VM, or serverless container.
  4. All-Cloud Foundation:
  5. Cloud Vector Database: Fully managed Zilliz Cloud (Serverless Milvus) via remote URI and API token.
  6. In-Process Fallback: Milvus Lite (uri="./milvus_data.db") runs natively inside Python for zero-setup local development.
  7. Cloud LLM & Embeddings: OpenAI (gpt-4o, gpt-4o-mini, text-embedding-3-small), Azure OpenAI (Azure AD credentials), or NVIDIA Cloud NIM endpoints (build.nvidia.com).
  8. BioContext MCP Integration:
  9. Standardized biomedical knowledge retrieved via BioContext Model Context Protocol (https://mcp.biocontext.ai/mcp/).
  10. Unified tools for OpenTargets (target-disease associations & tractability), KEGG (metabolic & disease pathways), Europe PMC (scientific literature), UniProt (protein sequences & functions), Ensembl (genomics), and PanglaoDB (single-cell markers).

docs.title: ⚙️ Environment Configuration
docs.text:
Set the following environment variables:

# ==========================================
# 1. Cloud LLM Configuration
# ==========================================
export OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-..."                 # Required for OpenAI models
# Or for Azure OpenAI:
# export AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT="https://your-resource.openai.azure.com/"
# export AZURE_OPENAI_DEPLOYMENT="your-deployment"
# export AZURE_CLIENT_ID="..."
# export AZURE_TENANT_ID="..."
# export AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET="..."
# Or for NVIDIA Cloud Endpoints:
# export NVIDIA_API_KEY="nvapi-..."

# ==========================================
# 2. Zero-Docker Cloud Vector Database
# ==========================================
# Option A: Zilliz Cloud (Fully Managed Cloud Milvus)
export MILVUS_URI="https://in03-xxxx.serverless.gcp-us-west1.cloud.zilliz.com"
export MILVUS_TOKEN="db_admin:YourZillizPassword"  # Or your Zilliz Cloud API Key

# Option B: Milvus Lite (Zero Docker, embedded local file)
# export MILVUS_URI="./milvus_data.db"
# (If MILVUS_URI is left empty, the system automatically falls back to Milvus Lite)

# ==========================================
# 3. BioContext MCP Cloud Gateway
# ==========================================
export BIOCONTEXT_MCP_URL="https://mcp.biocontext.ai/mcp/"

# ==========================================
# 4. Optional Agent Keys
# ==========================================
export ZOTERO_API_KEY="..."                    # For Lithoscribe
export ZOTERO_USER_ID="..."                    # For Lithoscribe

Synapta biocontext_kegg Maps disease and drug nodes to KEGG biological & metabolic pathways. Vivarix biocontext_kegg Cross-references reaction kinetics and enzymes with KEGG metabolic networks. docs.text:
# 1. Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/AtlasRoX/TribosAI
cd Tribos

# 2. Install dependencies (creates virtual environment automatically)
uv sync --extra dev --frozen

# 3. Set up pre-commit hooks (optional but recommended)

export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...

docs.title: Modern Python Stack
docs.text:
This project uses a modern Python development stack:

  • 📦 uv: Ultra-fast Python package manager and dependency resolver
  • 🏗️ hatchling: Modern build backend (PEP 621 compliant)
  • 📝 pyproject.toml: Single source of truth for project configuration
  • 🔒 uv.lock: Reproducible dependency resolution

docs.title: Why uv over pip/conda?
docs.text:
• 10-100x faster than pip for dependency resolution
  • Automatic virtual environment management
  • Built-in lock file support for reproducible builds
  • Better dependency conflict resolution
  • Native pyproject.toml support

docs.title: 📂 Project Structure
docs.text:
Tribos/
├── tribos/                   # Main package
│   ├── agents/               # Orchestrator, query planning, prompts, citations
│   ├── agentic/              # Agentic frameworks, Auto router, jobs, code sandbox
│   ├── archivon/             # Literature search and citation grounding
│   ├── axiom/                # Computer algebra and the verified mathematics agent
│   ├── dynamis/              # Numerical simulation and optimization

docs.title: Upload Security
docs.text: Uploads go to the API, never to a UI process: POST /api/datasets (app/backend/routers/datasets.py, tribos/datasets/) and POST /api/vision/read (app/backend/routers/vision.py). Both authenticate before the multipart body is parsed, refuse a Content-Length over the cap with 413, accept only listed extensions or image types, keep server-generated paths under the upload root (uploader file names are sanitized display names only) and validate the content before it is stored. GET /api/datasets/limits returns the accepted extensions and the per-kind caps (TRIBOS_UPLOAD_MAX_MB_*).
